docs.title: Logging: Your Model's Diary
docs.text:
print() statements are for interactive exploration. For any code that runs non-interactively, logging is the professional standard. A good logging setup provides a structured, configurable, and permanent record of your application's behavior.

Key Advantages of Logging: - Different Severity Levels: You can log messages at different levels (e.g., DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL), allowing you to filter for important events. - Configurability: You can easily redirect log output to a file, the console, or a remote service without changing your code. - Structured Information: Logs can be configured to automatically include timestamps, the function name, and the line number where the event occurred, making debugging much easier.

logger = logging.getLogger("MyEconomicModel")
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)  # Set the lowest level to capture all messages

# Create a handler to write logs to the console
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
formatter = logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s")
handler.setFormatter(formatter)

# Add the handler to the logger
if not logger.handlers:
    logger.addHandler(handler)

logger.info("Model initialization started.")
try:
    x = 1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    logger.error("An attempt to divide by zero occurred.", exc_info=True)
logger.debug("This is a detailed debug message for developers.")
print("> **Note:** Check the console output to see the structured log messages.")

docs.title: API Design: Serving Your Model
docs.text:
A research script might be run manually. A production model needs an Application Programming Interface (API) so that other services can interact with it programmatically. For economic models, this often means creating a web API where a user can send a request with new data and receive the model's prediction or forecast in response.

FastAPI is a modern, high-performance Python framework for building APIs. It is easy to use and provides automatic data validation and documentation.

(Conceptual Example - Code not runnable in notebook) 

## main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
import joblib # For loading a pre-trained model

app = FastAPI()
model = joblib.load('my_model.pkl')

class ModelInput(BaseModel):
    feature1: float
    feature2: int

@app.post('/predict')
def predict(data: ModelInput):
    prediction = model.predict([[data.feature1, data.feature2]])
    return {'prediction': prediction[0]}
You would run this with a server like uvicorn main:app --reload.

docs.title: Type Hinting for Scientific Code
docs.text:
Type hints (typing module) improve code clarity and catch errors before runtime. For scientific code, we often want to specify the shape and data type of arrays. While standard Python doesn't fully support this yet, libraries like numpy.typing (and jaxtyping) are making it possible.

from typing import Tuple
import numpy as np
from numpy.typing import NDArray

def calculate_returns(prices: NDArray[np.float64]) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
    """Calculates returns from a price array."""
    return prices[1:] / prices[:-1] - 1
Using these hints allows IDEs and static analysis tools (mypy) to warn you if you pass a list instead of an array.

docs.title: CI/CD: Automating Quality and Deployment
docs.text:
Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Deployment (CD) are practices that automate the process of testing and deploying code. We have already seen the CI part in Chapter 1.2 with GitHub Actions running our pytest suite.

  • Continuous Integration: Every time code is pushed to the repository, an automated pipeline runs to build the code, run tests, and check for quality issues. This ensures that bugs are caught early.
  • Continuous Deployment: If the CI pipeline passes, a CD pipeline can automatically deploy the new version of the application to a staging or production environment. This allows for rapid, reliable releases.

A full CI/CD pipeline for an economic model might look like this: 1. Commit: A developer pushes a change to the model's code. 2. CI Pipeline (GitHub Actions): a. Install dependencies from environment.yml. b. Run pytest to check for correctness. c. Run pre-commit hooks to check for style. d. (Optional) Build a Docker container for the application. 3. CD Pipeline: a. If CI passes on the main branch, automatically deploy the new version to a cloud server (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud).

Transitioning from research to production requires a shift in mindset. - Logging replaces printing for persistent, searchable records. - APIs allow your model to be consumed by other systems. - CI/CD automates the testing and deployment process, ensuring reliability and speed.

By adopting these practices, you ensure that your economic models can have a real-world impact.

docs.title: The Lens: The Engine of Computational Economics
docs.text:
What problem are we solving? Economics is the science of interconnected systems. A change in the Fed funds rate ripples through bond markets, mortgage rates, housing demand, and construction employment. A tariff on steel alters input costs for automakers, construction firms, and appliance manufacturers. To model these systems, we need a language that can handle simultaneity and dimensionality. Single equations are insufficient; we need systems of equations.

Why this method? Linear Algebra is that language. It provides the geometry and arithmetic for high-dimensional spaces. In computational economics, matrices are not just abstract arrays of numbers; they are the gears of our models: * The Jacobian Matrix encodes how a system evolves dynamically near a steady state. * The Hessian Matrix tells us if an optimal policy is a maximum or a minimum. * The Markov Matrix describes how agents move between states (e.g., employment to unemployment) over time.

This notebook moves beyond the textbook definitions to focus on the computational reality of linear algebra: numerical stability, the cost of inversion, and the power of decompositions like SVD.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this notebook, you will be able to: 1. Visualize linear transformations and understand the geometric meaning of determinants and eigenvalues. 2. Implement efficient and stable solutions to linear systems using scipy.linalg (avoiding explicit matrix inversion). 3. Diagnose ill-conditioned problems using the condition number. 4. Apply the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) for dimensionality reduction (PCA). 5. Utilize sparse matrices to handle large-scale economic networks efficiently.

docs.text:

Historical Context — Turing and Wilkinson make elimination trustworthy (1948–1961). Alan Turing's 1948 paper on rounding errors introduced conditioning and analyzed Gaussian elimination; James Wilkinson at NPL then built backward error analysis, explaining why pivoted elimination is reliable. EISPACK and LINPACK (1970s) encoded these results, LAPACK (1992) refactored them for caches — numpy.linalg calls their descendants today.

docs.title: 1. Vector Spaces, Subspaces, and Bases
docs.text:
A vector space is a collection of objects called vectors, which can be added together and multiplied by scalars. The familiar n-dimensional real space, \(\mathbb{R}^n\), is the canonical example in economics.

A subspace is a subset of a vector space that is itself a vector space. Crucially, it must contain the zero vector and be closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Linear Independence: A set of vectors \(\{v_1, ..., v_k\}\) is linearly independent if no vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others.
  • Span: The span of a set of vectors is the set of all possible linear combinations of those vectors.
  • Basis: A basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that span the space. It provides a unique coordinate system.
  • Dimension: The number of vectors in a basis.

docs.title: Inner Products, Norms, and Angles
docs.text: Vector spaces often come with a notion of geometry defined by the Inner Product (Dot Product): \(x \cdot y = \sum x_i y_i\). This induces: * Norm (Length): \(||x|| = \sqrt{x \cdot x}\) * Angle: \(\cos \theta = \frac{x \cdot y}{||x|| \cdot ||y||}\). For nonconstant data vectors, Pearson correlation is the cosine of the angle between their mean-centered versions. Orthogonal raw vectors need not be uncorrelated.

docs.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces
docs.text:
For any \(m \times n\) matrix \(A\), four fundamental subspaces describe its structure. The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra connects their dimensions:

  1. Column Space, \(C(A)\): The span of the columns of \(A\). Dimension = \(r\) (rank).
  2. Row Space, \(C(A^T)\): The span of the rows of \(A\). Dimension = \(r\).
  3. Null Space, \(N(A)\): Vectors \(x\) such that \(Ax = 0\). Dimension = \(n-r\).
  4. Left Null Space, \(N(A^T)\): Vectors \(y\) such that \(A^T y = 0\). Dimension = \(m-r\).

Orthogonality: \(C(A^T) \perp N(A)\) and \(C(A) \perp N(A^T)\).

Figure: The Big Picture of Linear Algebra (Strang). The Null Space is orthogonal to the Row Space.

docs.title: Application: Markov Chains and Steady States
docs.text:
Linear Algebra provides a direct way to solve for the long-run equilibrium of a system. Consider a labor market where agents move between Employment (E) and Unemployment (U).

Let \(x_t = [E_t, U_t]^T\). The dynamics are \(x_{t+1} = P^T x_t\), where \(P\) is the transition matrix. A steady state \(\pi\) satisfies \(\pi = P^T \pi\). This is an eigenvector problem: \(\pi\) is the eigenvector of \(P^T\) associated with eigenvalue \(\lambda=1\). The Perron-Frobenius Theorem guarantees that for a positive transition matrix, this eigenvector exists, is unique (up to scaling), and has positive entries.

# Transition Matrix P (Rows sum to 1)
#        E    U
# E [0.95, 0.05]  (5% separation rate)
# U [0.40, 0.60]  (40% finding rate)
P = np.array([[0.95, 0.05],
              [0.40, 0.60]])

# We need to solve (P.T - I) * pi = 0
# Or find the eigenvector of P.T with eigenvalue 1
evals, evecs = linalg.eig(P.T)

# Find the index of the eigenvalue close to 1
idx = np.argmin(np.abs(evals - 1.0))
pi = np.real(evecs[:, idx])

# Normalize to sum to 1 (probability distribution)
pi = pi / np.sum(pi)

print(f"Steady State Unemployment Rate: {pi[1]:.2%}")
print(f"Steady State Employment Rate:   {pi[0]:.2%}")

docs.title: Special Matrices in Economics
docs.text:
Certain matrix structures appear repeatedly in economic theory. Recognizing them allows us to use specialized, faster algorithms.

  1. Symmetric Matrices (\(A = A^T\)):

    • Where: Covariance matrices, Hessian matrices (second derivatives of utility/profit functions).
    • Property: All eigenvalues are real, and an orthonormal eigenbasis can be chosen. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

  2. Positive Definite Matrices:

    • Where: A valid covariance matrix must be positive semi-definite. For a twice-differentiable unconstrained objective, a local minimum requires a positive semi-definite Hessian. At a stationary point, positive definiteness is sufficient for a strict local minimum, but not necessary: \(f(x)=x^4\) has a strict minimum with \(f^{\prime\prime}(0)=0\).
    • Definition: \(x^T A x > 0\) for all non-zero vectors \(x\).
    • Check: All eigenvalues are positive.

    Cholesky Decomposition: A symmetric positive-definite matrix \(A\) can be uniquely factored as \(A = L L^T\), where \(L\) is a lower triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries. This is essentially a "square root" of a matrix. * Application: Generating correlated random variables. If \(z \sim N(0, I)\), then \(x = Lz + \mu\) follows \(N(\mu, \Sigma)\) where \(\Sigma = LL^T\).

  3. Idempotent Matrices (\(P^2 = P\)):

    • Where: Projection matrices in OLS (the "Hat Matrix").
    • Property: Eigenvalues are either 0 or 1.

  4. Orthogonal Matrices (\(Q^T Q = I\)):

    • Where: Rotations, QR decomposition, SVD.
    • Property: Preserves length (\(||Qx|| = ||x||\)) and angles.

docs.title: 2. Matrices as Linear Transformations
docs.text:
A matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) represents a linear transformation mapping \(\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\). Geometrically, it distorts space: it can rotate, scale, shear, or project vectors.

Figure: A linear transformation mapping a square to a parallelogram. The determinant of a square matrix, \(\det(A)\), measures the change in volume induced by the transformation. * If \(\det(A) = 2\), the transformation doubles the area (in 2D) or volume (in 3D) of any shape. * If \(\det(A) = 0\), the transformation squashes space into a lower dimension (e.g., a plane into a line). The matrix is singular (not invertible).

docs.title: 3. Solving Systems of Linear Equations: Ax = b
docs.text: The problem Ax = b asks: "What vector x, when transformed by A, lands on b?"

docs.title: Best Practice: solve > inv
docs.text:
In mathematical notation, we write \(x = A^{-1}b\). However, in numerical computing, you should almost never compute the inverse explicitly.

Computing x = inv(A) @ b is: 1. Slower: Inverting a matrix is computationally more expensive than solving the system. 2. Less Accurate: It introduces more floating-point round-off error.

Instead, use scipy.linalg.solve(A, b), which uses highly optimized decompositions (like LU factorization).

N = 2000
A = rng.random((N, N))
b = rng.random(N)

print(f"Solving system of size {N}x{N}...")

# 1. Using solve (The Right Way)
start = time.time()
x_solve = linalg.solve(A, b)
t_solve = time.time() - start
print(f"`linalg.solve`: {t_solve:.4f} seconds")

# 2. Using inverse (The Wrong Way)
start = time.time()
x_inv = linalg.inv(A) @ b
t_inv = time.time() - start
print(f"`linalg.inv`:   {t_inv:.4f} seconds")

print(f"Speedup: {t_inv / t_solve:.2f}x")

# Accuracy: compare the two answers (both are close here on a well-conditioned
# random matrix, but inv() carries extra round-off and costs ~2x the flops)
r_solve = np.linalg.norm(A @ x_solve - b)
r_inv = np.linalg.norm(A @ x_inv - b)
print(f"Residual ||Ax-b|| via solve: {r_solve:.3e}")
print(f"Residual ||Ax-b|| via inv:   {r_inv:.3e}")
print(f"Max abs difference between the two solutions: {np.max(np.abs(x_solve - x_inv)):.3e}")

docs.title: Application: The Leontief Input-Output Model
docs.text:
The Leontief model describes an economy where each sector requires inputs from other sectors to produce output. Let \(A\) be the technology matrix where \(A_{ij}\) is the input from sector \(i\) required to produce 1 unit of good \(j\). With \(n\) sectors, the dimensions are \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) and \(x, d \in \mathbb{R}^n\), while \(I = I_n\) is the \(n \times n\) identity — so \((I - A)\) is square, and the system below has a unique solution whenever it is nonsingular. Let \(d\) be the vector of final demand. The total gross output \(x\) required is:

\[ x = Ax + d \implies (I - A)x = d \]

We need to solve this linear system for \(x\).

docs.title: Application: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
docs.text:
In OLS, we want to find the vector \(\beta\) that minimizes the sum of squared residuals: \(||y - X\beta||^2\).

Derivation of Normal Equations: 1. Objective: \(L(\beta) = (y - X\beta)^T (y - X\beta)\) 2. Expand: \(L(\beta) = y^T y - \beta^T X^T y - y^T X \beta + \beta^T X^T X \beta\) 3. Derivative w.r.t. \(\beta\): \(\nabla_\beta L = -2 X^T y + 2 X^T X \beta\) 4. Set to zero: \(X^T X \beta = X^T y\)

Why is \(X^T X\) Symmetric Positive Semi-Definite? * Symmetric: \((X^T X)^T = X^T (X^T)^T = X^T X\). * Positive Semi-Definite: For any vector \(v\), \(v^T (X^T X) v = (Xv)^T (Xv) = ||Xv||^2 \ge 0\). This ensures the critical point is a minimum.

# Technology Matrix (3 sectors: Ag, Manuf, Svcs)
# e.g., A[0,1] = 0.2 means Manuf needs 0.2 units from Ag per unit of output
A = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.4],
              [0.5, 0.1, 0.3],
              [0.1, 0.6, 0.1]])

I = np.eye(3)
L = I - A # Leontief Matrix

# Scenario: Different final demands
d_scenario1 = np.array([100, 200, 500])

# Factorize L once (LU decomposition) to reuse for multiple solves
lu_piv = linalg.lu_factor(L)

x1 = linalg.lu_solve(lu_piv, d_scenario1)
print(f"Required Output (Scenario 1): {x1}")

docs.title: 4. Stability and the Condition Number
docs.text:
The condition number \(\kappa(A)\) measures how sensitive the solution \(x\) is to small changes in \(b\) or \(A\). $$ \kappa(A) = ||A|| \cdot ||A^{-1}|| $$

  • Well-conditioned (low \(\kappa\)): Small errors in inputs lead to small errors in outputs.
  • Ill-conditioned (high \(\kappa\)): Small errors can explode. This often happens in OLS when regressors are highly correlated (multicollinearity).
n = 100
x1 = rng.standard_normal(n)
# Create x2 highly correlated with x1
x2 = 0.999 * x1 + 0.001 * rng.standard_normal(n)

X = np.c_[np.ones(n), x1, x2]

# Compute condition number of X'X
cond_num = np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X)
print(f"Condition Number of X'X: {cond_num:.2e}")
print("Interpretation: This extremely high value indicates severe multicollinearity.")
print("OLS estimates will be unstable.")

docs.title: 5. Eigenvalues and System Dynamics
docs.text:
An eigenvector \(v\) of \(A\) is a vector that doesn't change direction when transformed by \(A\); it is only scaled by its eigenvalue \(\lambda\): $$ Av = \lambda v $$

Here \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\), each eigenvector satisfies \(v_i \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}\), and \(\lambda_i \in \mathbb{C}\). Eigenvalues govern the long-run behavior of dynamic systems \(x_{t+1} = Ax_t\). If \(A\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{C}\), we can write \(A = V \Lambda V^{-1}\) with eigenvector columns \(V = [v_1, \dots, v_n]\) and \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\), we get \(A^t = V \Lambda^t V^{-1}\), hence $$ x_t = A^t x_0 = V \Lambda^t V^{-1} x_0 = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \lambda_i^{\,t} v_i, \qquad c = V^{-1} x_0 \in \mathbb{C}^n, $$ a weighted sum of eigenvectors whose coefficients are determined at \(t=0\). Real matrices can have complex eigenvectors; conjugate pairs combine to give real trajectories. If \(A\) is defective, use Jordan or Schur form instead; the strict spectral-radius stability criterion below still holds. * If all \(|\lambda_i| < 1\), the terms \(\lambda_i^t \to 0\), so the system is stable (converges to steady state). If anyklzzwxh:0132, that term grows exponentially, making the system unstable**. * If mid, it exhibits saddle-path stability: only specific initial conditions (where the coefficients \(c_i\) for unstable modes are zero) lead to convergence.

Figure: Phase diagram showing stable, unstable, and saddle-path dynamics based on eigenvalues.

docs.title: Verbatim Walkthrough: Solving a 2x2 System
docs.text:
Let's unpack exactly how this decomposition works with a concrete example. Consider the system: $$ \begin{bmatrix} x_{t+1} \ y_{t+1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.2 \ 0.2 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_t \ y_t \end{bmatrix} $$

Step 1: Find Eigenvalues. Solve \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\). $$ \det \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 - \lambda & 0.2 \ 0.2 & 0.5 - \lambda \end{bmatrix} = (0.5 - \lambda)^2 - 0.04 = 0 $$ $$ (0.5 - \lambda)^2 = 0.04 \implies 0.5 - \lambda = \pm 0.2 $$ $$ \lambda_1 = 0.7, \quad \lambda_2 = 0.3 $$ Both are less than 1, so the system is stable.

Step 2: Find Eigenvectors. For \(\lambda_1 = 0.7\): \((A - 0.7I)v_1 = 0 \implies -0.2x + 0.2y = 0 \implies x=y\). So \(v_1 = [1, 1]^T\). For \(\lambda_2 = 0.3\): \((A - 0.3I)v_2 = 0 \implies 0.2x + 0.2y = 0 \implies x=-y\). So \(v_2 = [1, -1]^T\).

Step 3: General Solution. Any initial state \([x_0, y_0]^T\) can be written as \(c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2\). The state at time \(t\) is: $$ \begin{bmatrix} x_t \ y_t \end{bmatrix} = c_1 (0.7)^t \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 (0.3)^t \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ -1 \end{bmatrix} $$ Since \(0.7^t \to 0\) and \(0.3^t \to 0\), both \(x_t\) and \(y_t\) converge to 0.

This is the foundation of analyzing steady states in Macroeconomics (e.g., Blanchard-Kahn conditions).

docs.title: 6. The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
docs.text: The SVD is the "Swiss Army Knife" of linear algebra. It factors any matrix \(A\) into: $$ A = U \Sigma V^T $$ where \(\Sigma\) contains the singular values \(\sigma_i\). These values represent the "energy" or importance of each dimension.

docs.title: Application: Image Compression
docs.text:
We can approximate a matrix (an image) using only its largest singular values. This is a "low-rank approximation".

Deep Intuition: SVD works because it finds the "best" basis to represent the data. \(V\) rotates the data so that the first axis points in the direction of maximum variance (principal component), the second axis in the next largest variance, etc. \(\Sigma\) tells us how much variance is in each direction. Dropping small \(\sigma_i\) is just denoising.

docs.title: Application: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
docs.text:
In economics, PCA is used to summarize complex data. For example, the Yield Curve (interest rates at different maturities) is driven by three main factors: 1. Level: All rates move up/down together (1st Principal Component). 2. Slope: Short vs Long term rates change (2nd PC). 3. Curvature: Medium term rates bulge (3rd PC).

If \(X\) is our data matrix (centered), then the Right Singular Vectors (\(V\)) of \(X\) are exactly the Principal Components.

# Load sample image
img = face(gray=True)
img = img[::2, ::2] # Downsample for speed

# Compute SVD
U, s, Vt = linalg.svd(img, full_matrices=False)

def compress(k: int, U, s, Vt):
    """Reconstruct image using top k singular values."""
    S_k = np.diag(s[:k])
    return U[:, :k] @ S_k @ Vt[:k, :]

# Visualize
k_values = [5, 20, 50, 100]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(k_values)+1, figsize=(15, 4))

axes[0].imshow(img, cmap='gray')
axes[0].set_title("Original")
axes[0].axis('off')

for i, k in enumerate(k_values):
    img_k = compress(k, U, s, Vt)
    axes[i+1].imshow(img_k, cmap='gray')
    axes[i+1].set_title(f"k={k}")
    axes[i+1].axis('off')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: 7. Sparse Matrices
docs.text:
Economic networks (e.g., input-output, social graphs) are often sparse: most connections are zero. Storing these as dense arrays wastes memory.

scipy.sparse stores only non-zero elements.

N = 5000
# Tridiagonal discretization of a 1D Laplacian (e.g., finite-difference Hessian)
main_diag = -2.0 * np.ones(N)
off_diag = np.ones(N - 1)
A_sparse = sparse.diags(
    diagonals=[off_diag, main_diag, off_diag], offsets=[-1, 0, 1], format="csr"
)

print(f"Sparse Matrix Memory: {A_sparse.data.nbytes / 1e6:.2f} MB")
# Dense equivalent would be N*N*8 bytes ~ 200MB
print(f"Dense Equivalent:     {(N*N*8) / 1e6:.2f} MB")

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
These relations are collected from the derivations above as a review map. Their assumptions and derivations remain part of the result; this box is not a substitute for them.

1. Core relation

\[x = Ax + d \implies (I - A)x = d\]

2. Core relation

\[\kappa(A) = ||A|| \cdot ||A^{-1}||\]

3. Core relation

\[Av = \lambda v\]

4. Core relation

\[\begin{bmatrix} x_{t+1} \\ y_{t+1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_t \\ y_t \end{bmatrix}\]

Dimension notes: (1) Leontief: \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\), \(x, d \in \mathbb{R}^n\). (2) Condition number: \(\kappa(A) \ge 1\) is a dimensionless scalar. (3) Eigenpair: \(v \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}\), \(\lambda \in \mathbb{C}\). (4) Linear system: state \(\in \mathbb{R}^2\), transition matrix \(2 \times 2\).

docs.title: Economic Interpretation: Why conditioning is an economic issue
docs.text: In an estimated equilibrium system, a large condition number means that small sampling, calibration, or rounding errors in moments and coefficients can produce economically large changes in the recovered prices, quantities, or policy coefficients. Decompositions such as QR and SVD are therefore not only numerical conveniences: they diagnose weakly identified directions and distinguish economically meaningful variation from nearly redundant equations.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Key Takeaways: * Think Geometrically: Matrices are linear transformations. * Solve, Don't Invert: Use scipy.linalg.solve for speed and stability. * Watch the Condition Number: High \(\kappa(A)\) means unreliable results. * SVD is Powerful: It reveals the underlying structure and rank of data. * Go Sparse: For large networks, sparse matrices are essential.

Common Pitfalls in This Lecture

  • Explicit inverses. np.linalg.inv(A) @ b is slower and less accurate than np.linalg.solve(A, b), which factors once and never forms the inverse. Also, inv fails outright on singular matrices that lstsq would handle gracefully.
  • Trusting near-solutions. A matrix can be technically invertible yet numerically useless: \(\kappa(A) \approx 10^{12}\) means you lose ~12 digits of precision. Inspect the condition number before interpreting any solution of an ill-conditioned system.

docs.title: 1. Conceptual: The Idempotent Matrix
docs.text: An idempotent matrix \(P\) satisfies \(P^2 = P\). In econometrics, the projection matrix \(P = X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\) is idempotent. Prove that the eigenvalues of an idempotent matrix must be either 0 or 1.

docs.title: 2. Applied: QR Decomposition for OLS
docs.text: A numerically stable way to solve the OLS problem \((X^TX)\beta = X^Ty\) is using QR Decomposition (\(X = QR\)). * Task: Generate a random design matrix X and target y. Compute \(\beta\) using scipy.linalg.qr and solve_triangular. Compare the result with scipy.linalg.lstsq. * Hint: The normal equations simplify to \(R\beta = Q^T y\).

docs.title: 3. Challenge: Google's PageRank
docs.text:
PageRank models the web as a Markov chain. The PageRank vector \(v\) is the principal eigenvector of the Google matrix \(G\), satisfying \(Gv = v\) (eigenvalue \(\lambda=1\)). * Task: Create a random 100x100 transition matrix representing web links. Damping factor \(\alpha=0.85\). Use the Power Iteration method to find the steady-state vector \(v\). Visualize the convergence of the error over iterations.

Failure analysis (Challenge): Solving an input-output system with inv(A) @ b returns a solution whose residual is large even though \(A\) is technically invertible. Diagnose ill-conditioning by computing \(\kappa(A)\), repair with solve/lstsq plus row scaling, and report the residual before and after alongside the digits lost.

docs.title: 02 Numerical Preliminaries
docs.text:
Source notebook: 02-Numerical-Methods/02_Numerical_Preliminaries.ipynb

Notebook outputs are intentionally omitted from the documentation build; code and narrative remain source-faithful.

docs.title: The Lens: The Illusion of Continuity
docs.text:
What problem are we solving? Economic theory deals with continuous variables: prices, quantities, probabilities. We write models using real numbers (\(\mathbb{R}\)). But computers are discrete machines. They cannot represent the continuum. They approximate real numbers using floating-point arithmetic, which introduces small but cumulative errors.

Why this method? Understanding the limitations of the machine is the first step in computational economics. * Machine Epsilon: The gap between 1.0 and the next representable float — a measure of relative precision (absolute spacing grows with magnitude). * Round-off Error: The error introduced by finite precision. * Truncation Error: The error introduced by approximating an infinite process (like a limit) with a finite one.

This notebook is about "knowing your tools." Before we solve complex models, we must understand how the computer counts.

Economic question. In 02 Numerical Preliminaries, what must remain economically invariant when the computational representation changes? In economic computation, an algorithm is part of the model: convergence tolerances, conditioning, discretization, and stopping rules can alter the apparent equilibrium. The central question is therefore not merely whether a routine returns a number, but whether that number is stable under tighter tolerances, alternative initial conditions, and an independent method. Treat every numerical result as an approximation with a measurable error budget.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this notebook, you will be able to: 1. Explain how computers represent numbers using IEEE 754 standard. 2. Quantify numerical errors (Absolute, Relative, Round-off, Truncation). 3. Diagnose stability and conditioning issues in algorithms. 4. Implement arbitrary-precision arithmetic when necessary. 5. Analyze the algorithmic complexity (Big-O) of your code.

docs.title: 1.1 IEEE 754 Floating-Point Representation
docs.text:
A standard 64-bit float (float64 in NumPy) consists of: 1. Sign Bit (1 bit): Positive or negative. 2. Exponent (11 bits): Magnitude range. 3. Mantissa (52 bits): Precision (significant digits).

For a normal finite value with stored exponent \(1 \le e \le 2046\) and stored 52-bit fraction integer \(m\),

\[x=(-1)^s(1+m/2^{52})2^{e-1023}.\]

The code below prints \(m\) as an integer, not the fraction \(m/2^{52}\). Exponent \(e=0\) encodes zeros and subnormals (no implicit leading 1); \(e=2047\) encodes infinities and NaNs.

Consequence: Numbers like 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary, leading to 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.

def float_to_bits(f):
    """Unpacks a 64-bit float into its sign, exponent, and mantissa bits."""
    packed = struct.pack('!d', f)
    integers = struct.unpack('!Q', packed)[0]
    # Extract bits
    sign = (integers >> 63) & 1
    exponent = (integers >> 52) & 0x7FF
    mantissa = integers & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFF
    return sign, exponent, mantissa

s, e, m = float_to_bits(19.94)
print("Float: 19.94")
print(f"Sign: {s}")
print(f"Exponent: {e} (Stored)")
print(f"Mantissa: {m}")

docs.title: 1.2 Machine Epsilon
docs.text:
Machine Epsilon (\(\epsilon_{mach}\)) is the distance from 1.0 to the next largest representable float. For 64-bit floats, \(\epsilon_{mach} \approx 2.22 \times 10^{-16}\).

Crucially, the spacing between floats is not uniform. It grows with magnitude. The gap between 1.0 and 2.0 is small; the gap between \(10^{16}\) and the next number is large (> 1.0).

docs.title: 1.3 Special Values: Infinity and NaN
docs.text:
The IEEE 754 standard reserves specific bit patterns for non-real results: * Infinity (inf): Can result from NumPy overflow (np.exp(1000.0)) or nonzero division by zero (np.divide(1.0, 0.0)), normally with a runtime warning. Python scalar 1.0 / 0.0 instead raises ZeroDivisionError. * Not a Number (nan): Results from invalid NumPy operations such as np.divide(0.0, 0.0) or np.inf - np.inf. Python scalar 0.0 / 0.0 raises ZeroDivisionError. * Warning: nan != nan. Always use np.isnan() to check.

eps = np.finfo(float).eps
print(f"Machine Epsilon: {eps:.2e}")

gap_at_1 = np.nextafter(1.0, 2.0) - 1.0
gap_at_large = np.nextafter(1e16, 2e16) - 1e16

print(f"Gap at 1.0:      {gap_at_1:.2e}")
print(f"Gap at 1e16:     {gap_at_large:.2f}")
print("Notice: At 1e16, the computer cannot represent odd integers!")

docs.title: 2. A Taxonomy of Numerical Error
docs.text:
1. Rounding Error: Caused by finite precision (e.g., storing \(\pi\) as a float).
  2. Truncation Error: Caused by approximating an infinite process (e.g., Taylor series, iterative limit) with a finite one.

docs.title: Absolute vs. Relative Error
docs.text:
• Absolute: \(E_{abs} = |x_{true} - x_{approx}|\)
  • Relative: \(E_{rel} = \frac{|x_{true} - x_{approx}|}{|x_{true}|}\)

docs.title: Forward vs. Backward Error
docs.text:
This distinction is crucial for stability analysis: * Forward Error: The difference between the computed answer and the true answer (\(|y_{computed} - y_{true}|\)). This is what we usually care about. * Backward Error: The size of the perturbation to the input that would make the computed answer the exact answer for that perturbed input. If an algorithm has small backward error, it is "Backward Stable". It gives the right answer to a slightly wrong problem.

Error Propagation Formula: If \(x_{approx} = x (1 + \epsilon_x)\) and \(y_{approx} = y (1 + \epsilon_y)\): * Multiplication: \(x_{approx} y_{approx} \approx xy(1 + \epsilon_x + \epsilon_y)\). Relative errors add. * Addition: \(x_{approx} + y_{approx} = (x+y) + x\epsilon_x + y\epsilon_y\). Relative error is \(\frac{x\epsilon_x + y\epsilon_y}{x+y}\). If \(x \approx -y\), the denominator is small, and error explodes (Cancellation).

Figure: Visualizing the trade-off between truncation error and round-off error. As the step size gets too small, round-off error dominates.

Best Practice: Always use relative error (or np.isclose which handles both) unless the value is near zero.

docs.title: 3.1 Conditioning (The Problem)
docs.text: A problem is ill-conditioned if small changes in inputs cause huge changes in outputs. Example: Solving \(Ax=b\) with a Hilbert matrix.

docs.title: 3.2 Stability (The Algorithm)
docs.text:
An algorithm is unstable if it amplifies rounding errors. Example: Catastrophic Cancellation when subtracting two nearly equal numbers.

# Demonstrating Catastrophic Cancellation in Variance Calculation
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
# Large mean, small variance
x = rng.normal(1e9, 1.0, size=10000)

# Naive formula: E[x^2] - (E[x])^2
var_naive = np.mean(x**2) - np.mean(x)**2

# Stable formula (NumPy's implementation)
var_stable = np.var(x)

print("True Variance:   1.0 (approx)")
print(f"Stable Var:      {var_stable:.4f}")
print(f"Naive Var:       {var_naive:.4f} (Often completely wrong or negative!)")

# Demonstrating Catastrophic Cancellation in Quadratic Formula
# Equation: ax^2 + bx + c = 0. Roots: (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a
# If b^2 >> |4ac|, then sqrt(b^2 - 4ac) ~ b, so (-b + sqrt(...))
# subtracts two nearly equal numbers and most digits are lost.
a = 1.0
b = 1.0e8
c = 1.0

# Naive Standard Formula for the smaller root (requires subtraction)
root_naive = (-b + np.sqrt(b**2 - 4*a*c)) / (2*a)

# Rationalized Formula (avoids subtraction)
root_stable = -2*c / (b + np.sqrt(b**2 - 4*a*c))

print(f"Naive Root:  {root_naive}")
print(f"Stable Root: {root_stable}")
print(f"Relative error of the naive root: {abs(root_naive - root_stable) / abs(root_stable):.1%}")

# Example: Loss of Significance in Finance
# Subtracting two large, nearly identical numbers (e.g., bond prices) results in loss of precision.
price_A = 100000.000000001
price_B = 100000.000000000

# Each input near 1e5 carries ~16 significant digits but has an
# absolute rounding uncertainty of about half an ulp (~7e-12).
# Their tiny difference inherits that same absolute uncertainty,
# so only about two of its digits are trustworthy.
diff = price_A - price_B
print(f"Difference: {diff}")
print("Most digits were lost in the subtraction: the inputs are each uncertain by ~1e-11, so this ~1e-9 difference keeps only ~2 reliable significant digits.")

docs.title: Kahan Summation Algorithm
docs.text:
When summing many numbers (like computing the mean of a large dataset), rounding errors accumulate: naive left-to-right addition has a worst-case error that grows linearly with the number of terms \(n\). Kahan summation keeps a separate compensation variable that captures the low-order bits lost at each addition and feeds them back into the next one:

y = x - c           # adjust the input by the prior compensation
t = s + y           # rounded sum
c = (t - s) - y     # recovers exactly the bits that rounding just discarded
s = t

This shrinks the accumulated error from \(O(n\,\epsilon_{mach})\) to roughly \(O(\epsilon_{mach})\), independent of \(n\). In practice, prefer battle-tested implementations: math.fsum returns the correctly rounded sum, and NumPy's np.sum tames error growth via pairwise (blocked) summation.

docs.title: 4. Arbitrary-Precision Arithmetic
docs.text:
For finance (where every penny counts) or high-precision math, standard floats are insufficient. Python's decimal module represents finite decimal inputs exactly when constructed from strings; operations still round to the active context precision. For example, Decimal('1') / Decimal('3') is not exact. Set precision and rounding rules explicitly for the calculation.

val_float = 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 - 0.3
print(f"Float Math:   {val_float:.20f} (Not zero!)")

val_decimal = Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.1') - Decimal('0.3')
print(f"Decimal Math: {val_decimal} (Exact)")

docs.title: 5. Rates of Convergence
docs.text:
When iterating (e.g., to find a root \(x^*\)), how fast does the error \(\epsilon_k = |x_k - x^*|\) shrink?

  1. Linear Convergence: \(\epsilon_{k+1} \le C \epsilon_k\) with \(C < 1\). The number of correct digits increases by a constant amount each step. (e.g., Bisection).
  2. Quadratic Convergence: \(\epsilon_{k+1} \le C \epsilon_k^2\). The number of correct digits doubles each step. (e.g., Newton's Method).

Quadratic is much faster. If \(\epsilon_k = 10^{-2}\), then \(\epsilon_{k+1} \approx 10^{-4}\), \(\epsilon_{k+2} \approx 10^{-8}\).

docs.title: 6. Algorithmic Complexity
docs.text:
Big-O Notation describes how runtime scales with input size \(N\).

  • \(O(1)\): Constant (Dictionary lookup).
  • \(O(N)\): Linear (Looping through a list).
  • \(O(N \log N)\): Log-Linear (Sorting, FFT). Crucial for efficient heterogeneous agent models.
  • \(O(N^2)\): Quadratic (Nested loops, matrix-vector multiplication).
  • \(O(N^3)\): Cubic (Matrix multiplication/inversion). Common in econometrics (OLS).

Figure: Growth rates of different complexity classes. Notice how fast exponential time explodes.

docs.title: Amortized Analysis
docs.text: Some operations are expensive occasionally but cheap on average. * Example: Appending to a Python list. Usually \(O(1)\), but occasionally \(O(N)\) when the memory buffer fills up and the list must be copied. The amortized cost is \(O(1)\).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Key Takeaways: * Floats are approximations: Use np.isclose with problem-appropriate tolerances for approximate numerical results; exact equality is still appropriate when exact identity is intended. * Conditioning Matters: A stable algorithm cannot fix an ill-conditioned problem. * Avoid Cancellation: Rewrite formulas (like variance or the quadratic formula) to avoid subtracting nearly equal numbers. * Know the Cost: Be aware of the Big-O complexity of your operations, especially inside loops.

docs.title: Appendix: Visualizing the Floating Point Gap
docs.text:
To really internalize the density of floating point numbers, let's visualize them. Notice how they are dense near zero and become sparse as magnitude increases.

# Visualizing 4-bit Floats (Toy Example)
# Assume 1 bit sign, 2 bits exponent, 1 bit mantissa for visualization

def get_toy_floats():
    values = []
    # Sign: 0 (pos) or 1 (neg)
    for s in [0, 1]:
        sign = (-1)**s
        # Exponent: 0 to 3. Bias = 1.
        for e in range(4):
            exponent = 2**(e - 1)
            # Mantissa: 0 or 1. (1 + m/2)
            for m in range(2):
                mantissa = 1 + m/2
                val = sign * mantissa * exponent
                values.append(val)
    return sorted(list(set(values)))

toy_vals = get_toy_floats()

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 2))
plt.scatter(toy_vals, np.zeros_like(toy_vals), marker='|', s=1000, c='k')
plt.xlim(-5, 5)
plt.ylim(-0.1, 0.1)
plt.yticks([])
plt.title("The Floating Point Number Line (Toy Model)")
plt.xlabel("Value")
plt.annotate('Dense near zero', xy=(0, 0), xytext=(0, 0.05), ha='center', arrowprops=dict(facecolor='black', shrink=0.05))
plt.annotate('Sparse further out', xy=(3, 0), xytext=(3, 0.05), ha='center', arrowprops=dict(facecolor='black', shrink=0.05))
plt.show()

docs.title: 03 Numerical Differentiation
docs.text:
Source notebook: 02-Numerical-Methods/03_Numerical_Differentiation.ipynb

Notebook outputs are intentionally omitted from the documentation build; code and narrative remain source-faithful.

docs.title: The Lens: The Calculus of the Discrete
docs.text:
What problem are we solving? In economics, we constantly need derivatives. Marginal utility is a derivative (\(u'(c)\)). Marginal cost is a derivative (\(C'(q)\)). The first-order condition for optimality sets a derivative to zero. But computers don't know calculus rules; they only know arithmetic. How do we compute a derivative without an analytical formula?

Why this method? We have two main approaches: 1. Finite Differences: Approximate the derivative using the slope between two nearby points. Simple, but prone to errors. 2. Automatic Differentiation (AD): The modern "magic" behind deep learning (JAX, PyTorch). It computes exact derivatives by decomposing code into a graph of elementary operations.

This notebook moves from the classical approximations to the modern powerhouse of AD.

Economic question. In 03 Numerical Differentiation, what must remain economically invariant when the computational representation changes? In economic computation, an algorithm is part of the model: convergence tolerances, conditioning, discretization, and stopping rules can alter the apparent equilibrium. The central question is therefore not merely whether a routine returns a number, but whether that number is stable under tighter tolerances, alternative initial conditions, and an independent method. Treat every numerical result as an approximation with a measurable error budget.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this notebook, you will be able to: 1. Implement Forward, Backward, and Central difference methods. 2. Analyze the trade-off between truncation error and round-off error (the step-size dilemma). 3. Use JAX to compute exact gradients and Hessians automatically. 4. Solve a utility maximization problem using Newton's method with JAX derivatives.

docs.title: 1. Numerical Differentiation via Finite Differences
docs.text: The derivative is defined as \(f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\). Numerically, we just pick a small \(h\). Throughout, \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is smooth and the step \(h \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}\); every estimate below approximates the scalar \(f'(x) \in \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: 1.1 The Formulas
docs.text:
1. Forward Difference: \(D_+ f(x) = \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\). Error: \(O(h)\).
  2. Backward Difference: \(D_- f(x) = \frac{f(x) - f(x-h)}{h}\). Error: \(O(h)\).
  3. Central Difference: \(D_c f(x) = \frac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h}\). Error: \(O(h^2)\).

Why Central is Better: By looking both ways, the first-order error terms cancel out, giving significantly higher accuracy for the same step size.

docs.title: Derivation via Taylor Series
docs.text:
Figure: Finite-difference error as the step size shrinks.. Expand \(f(x+h)\) and \(f(x-h)\): 1. \(f(x+h) = f(x) + hf'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2}f''(x) + \frac{h^3}{6}f'''(x) + \dots\) 2. \(f(x-h) = f(x) - hf'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2}f''(x) - \frac{h^3}{6}f'''(x) + \dots\)

Subtracting (2) from (1): $$ f(x+h) - f(x-h) = 2hf'(x) + \frac{h^3}{3}f'''(x) + \dots $$ Dividing by \(2h\) gives: $$ \frac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h} = f'(x) + \frac{h^2}{6}f'''(x) + \dots $$ The error term starts with \(h^2\), hence it is \(O(h^2)\).

docs.title: Richardson Extrapolation
docs.text:
We can eliminate the \(O(h^2)\) error term to get an \(O(h^4)\) approximation. Let \(D(h)\) be the central difference estimate with step \(h\). The error is approximately \(C h^2\). 1. \(D(h) \approx f'(x) + C h^2\) 2. \(D(h/2) \approx f'(x) + C (h/2)^2 = f'(x) + \frac{1}{4} C h^2\)

Multiply (2) by 4 and subtract (1): $$ 4D(h/2) - D(h) \approx 3f'(x) $$ $$ D_{richardson} = \frac{4D(h/2) - D(h)}{3} = f'(x) + O(h^4) $$

def forward_diff(f, x, h=1e-5):
    return (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h

def backward_diff(f, x, h=1e-5):
    return (f(x) - f(x - h)) / h

def central_diff(f, x, h=1e-5):
    return (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 * h)

# Test on f(x) = e^x at x=1 (True derivative is e^1)
f = np.exp
x0 = 1.0
true_val = np.exp(1.0)

print(f"True Value:     {true_val:.8f}")
print(f"Forward (h=1e-4): {forward_diff(f, x0, h=1e-4):.8f}")
print(f"Backward (h=1e-4): {backward_diff(f, x0, h=1e-4):.8f}")
print(f"Central (h=1e-4): {central_diff(f, x0, h=1e-4):.8f} (Much Closer!)")

docs.title: 1.2 The Step Size Dilemma
docs.text:
Choosing h involves a painful trade-off: * Truncation Error: Increases as h gets larger (math approximation error). * Round-off Error: Increases as h gets smaller (floating-point cancellation error).

There is a "Goldilocks" zone, typically around \(h \approx \sqrt{\epsilon_{mach}}\) for forward difference and \(h \approx \epsilon_{mach}^{1/3}\) for central difference.

Why these scales? Rounding noise in a difference quotient behaves like \(\epsilon_{mach}/h\): subtracting nearby values leaves only a few machine-accurate bits in the numerator, which dividing by a tiny \(h\) amplifies. Balancing that against truncation gives the optimum: \(O(h)\) truncation yields \(h \sim \sqrt{\epsilon_{mach}}\), while the central difference's \(O(h^2)\) truncation yields \(h \sim \epsilon_{mach}^{1/3}\).

docs.title: 2. Automatic Differentiation (AD)
docs.text:
AD is not numerical differentiation (finite differences) and it is not symbolic differentiation (Mathematica).

AD computes the exact derivative (up to machine precision) by applying the Chain Rule to every elementary operation in your code. It builds a computational graph and passes derivatives through it.

docs.title: Forward vs. Reverse Mode
docs.text:
• Forward Mode: Good for functions \(f: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n\) with few inputs relative to outputs (\(m \ll n\)).
  • Reverse Mode (Backprop): Good for functions \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) (many inputs, one output).

Economic Context: Most economic problems (Optimization, Maximum Likelihood) involve a scalar objective function with many parameters (\(n \gg 1\)). Thus, Reverse Mode (Backprop) is the standard.

docs.title: JVP vs VJP (The Heart of AD)
docs.text: This distinction explains the efficiency: * JVP (Jacobian-Vector Product): Computes \(Jv\) (directional derivative). This is Forward Mode. One pass gives one column of the Jacobian. Cost scales with inputs \(N\). * VJP (Vector-Jacobian Product): Computes \(v^TJ\) (gradient of linear combination). This is Reverse Mode. One pass gives one row of the Jacobian (the full gradient for scalar output). Cost scales with outputs \(M\).

docs.title: Complex Step Differentiation
docs.text: There is a "magic" trick for functions that can handle complex numbers (like NumPy's exp, sin). Consider the Taylor expansion of \(f(x+ih)\): $$ f(x+ih) = f(x) + ih f'(x) - \frac{h^2}{2} f''(x) - i\frac{h^3}{6} f'''(x) + \dots $$ Taking the imaginary part: $$ \text{Im}(f(x+ih)) = h f'(x) - \frac{h^3}{6} f'''(x) + \dots $$ $$ f'(x) \approx \frac{\text{Im}(f(x+ih))}{h} $$ This has no subtraction! We can make \(h\) extremely small (e.g., \(10^{-100}\)) without any cancellation error, achieving near-exact derivatives.

docs.title: Computational Graph
docs.text:
Consider \(y = \ln(x_1) + x_1 x_2\). 1. \(v_1 = \ln(x_1)\) 2. \(v_2 = x_1 x_2\) 3. \(y = v_1 + v_2\)

AD propagates derivatives through this graph via the Chain Rule.

docs.title: Code: Manual Backpropagation
docs.text:
To demystify AD, let's implement a tiny "autograd" engine. We define a Node class that knows its value and how to compute the derivative of its parents.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, parents=None, grad_fn=None):
        self.value = value
        self.parents = parents or []
        self.grad_fn = grad_fn # How to propagate gradient to parents
        self.grad = 0.0

    def backward(self, grad=1.0):
        self.grad += grad
        if self.grad_fn:
            self.grad_fn(grad)  # propagate only this contribution, not the accumulated total

    def __add__(self, other):
        # y = a + b => dy/da = 1, dy/db = 1
        def grad_fn(g):
            self.backward(g)
            other.backward(g)
        return Node(self.value + other.value, [self, other], grad_fn)

    def __mul__(self, other):
        # y = a * b => dy/da = b, dy/db = a
        def grad_fn(g):
            self.backward(g * other.value)
            other.backward(g * self.value)
        return Node(self.value * other.value, [self, other], grad_fn)

# Usage:
# x = Node(2.0); y = Node(3.0); z = x * y + x
# z.backward() 
# print(x.grad) # Should be y + 1 = 4
# Shared intermediate: x = Node(2.0); u = x * x; z = u + u
# z.backward(); print(x.grad) # 8, since z = 2*x**2

docs.title: Verbatim Walkthrough: Building AutoDiff from Scratch
docs.text: Let's build the Forward Mode ourselves using Dual Numbers — the clearest way to see what JAX does under the hood.

docs.title: Intuition: Dual Numbers (Forward Mode)
docs.text:
Forward mode can be understood using Dual Numbers of the form \(v + \dot{v}\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon^2 = 0\). This is similar to complex numbers (\(i^2 = -1\)). We define elementary arithmetic: \((a + \dot{a}\epsilon) + (b + \dot{b}\epsilon) = (a+b) + (\dot{a}+\dot{b})\epsilon\) and \((a + \dot{a}\epsilon)(b + \dot{b}\epsilon) = ab + (a\dot{b} + b\dot{a})\epsilon\). Notice that the \(\epsilon\) term automatically carries the derivative rule (product rule in the second case). If we evaluate \(f(x + 1\epsilon)\), the result is \(f(x) + f'(x)\epsilon\). The coefficient of \(\epsilon\) is the exact derivative!

class Dual:
    def __init__(self, value, grad=0.0):
        self.val = value
        self.grad = grad

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Dual(val={self.val}, grad={self.grad})"

    def __add__(self, other):
        # (a + be) + (c + de) = (a+c) + (b+d)e
        # Derivative of sum is sum of derivatives
        if isinstance(other, Dual):
            return Dual(self.val + other.val, self.grad + other.grad)
        return Dual(self.val + other, self.grad) # Constant

    def __mul__(self, other):
        # (a + be) * (c + de) = ac + (ad + bc)e + bd(e^2=0)
        # This is exactly the Product Rule: (uv)' = uv' + vu'
        if isinstance(other, Dual):
            new_val = self.val * other.val
            new_grad = self.val * other.grad + self.grad * other.val
            return Dual(new_val, new_grad)
        return Dual(self.val * other, self.grad * other)

    def sin(self):
        # Chain rule: sin(a + be) = sin(a) + cos(a)*b*e
        return Dual(np.sin(self.val), np.cos(self.val) * self.grad)

# Let's differentiate f(x) = x * sin(x) at x=2
x = Dual(2.0, 1.0) # 1.0 seeds the derivative (dx/dx = 1)
y = x * x.sin()

print(f"Function Value: {y.val:.4f}")
print(f"Derivative:     {y.grad:.4f}")

# Verify with analytical rule: sin(x) + x*cos(x)
true_grad = np.sin(2.0) + 2.0 * np.cos(2.0)
print(f"True Deriv:     {true_grad:.4f}")

docs.title: Code: Complex Step vs Finite Difference
docs.text:
# Demonstrating the stability of Complex Step
def g(x): return np.exp(x) / np.sin(x)**3

x0 = 1.5
h_vals = [1e-5, 1e-10, 1e-15, 1e-20]

print(f"{'h':<10} | {'Finite Diff Error':<20} | {'Complex Step Error':<20}")
print("-"*55)

# Analytical derivative via the quotient rule (exact)
true_val = (np.exp(x0)*np.sin(x0)**3 - 3*np.exp(x0)*np.sin(x0)**2*np.cos(x0)) / np.sin(x0)**6

for h in h_vals:
    fd_val = (g(x0+h) - g(x0))/h
    cs_val = np.imag(g(x0 + 1j*h))/h

    print(f"{h:<10.0e} | {abs(fd_val - true_val):<20.2e} | {abs(cs_val - true_val):<20.2e}")

print("Observation: once h gets tiny, cancellation makes the finite-difference error balloon, while Complex Step stays near machine precision.")

docs.title: 3. The JAX Framework
docs.text:
JAX is a Google library that combines NumPy, Automatic Differentiation, and GPU/TPU acceleration. It is becoming the standard for high-performance computational economics.

Key transformations: * grad(f): Computes the gradient. * jit(f): Just-In-Time compiles the function for speed. * vmap(f): Automatically vectorizes a function.

docs.title: The Constraint of Pure Functions
docs.text:
JAX transforms require pure functions: 1. Deterministic: Same input \(\to\) Same output. (No global random state). 2. No Side Effects: No printing, no writing to files, no modifying global variables.

If you violate this, the JIT compiler will optimize away your side effects or produce unpredictable results.

if JAX_AVAILABLE:
    # 1. Define a function using JAX numpy
    def f(x):
        return jnp.sin(x) * jnp.exp(-x)

    # 2. Transform it to get gradient and hessian functions
    df = grad(f)
    d2f = hessian(f)

    # 3. Evaluate
    x_val = 1.0
    print(f"f(1.0):    {f(x_val):.6f}")
    print(f"f'(1.0):   {df(x_val):.6f} (Exact)")
    print(f"f''(1.0):  {d2f(x_val):.6f} (Exact)")

    # 4. JIT Compile for speed
    df_fast = jit(df)
    _ = df_fast(x_val) # Trigger compilation
    print("JIT-compiled gradient is ready.")

docs.title: 4. Application: Utility Maximization
docs.text:
Let's solve a consumer problem: Maximize CES utility subject to a budget constraint. $$ \max_{c_1, c_2} (c_1^\rho + c_2^\rho)^{1/\rho} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p_1 c_1 + p_2 c_2 = M $$

We will solve the First-Order Conditions (FOCs) using Newton's Method, where the Jacobian is computed via JAX.

if JAX_AVAILABLE:
    # Parameters
    p1, p2, M = 2.0, 3.0, 100.0
    rho = 0.5

    # The Lagrangian: L(c1, c2, lam)
    def lagrangian(x):
        c1, c2, lam = x[0], x[1], x[2]
        utility = (c1**rho + c2**rho)**(1/rho)
        constraint = p1*c1 + p2*c2 - M
        return utility - lam * constraint

    # We want to find x such that gradient of Lagrangian is zero
    # FOC function returns the gradient vector
    foc_func = jit(grad(lagrangian))
    # Jacobian of FOCs is the Hessian of the Lagrangian
    jacobian_foc = jit(hessian(lagrangian))

    # Newton's Method
    x = jnp.array([10.0, 10.0, 0.5]) # Initial guess [c1, c2, lambda]

    print("Starting Newton's Method...")
    for i in range(10):
        F = foc_func(x)
        J = jacobian_foc(x)

        # Update: x_new = x_old - J^-1 * F
        step = jnp.linalg.solve(J, -F)
        x = x + step

        error = jnp.linalg.norm(step)
        if error < 1e-8:
            print(f"Converged in {i+1} iterations.")
            break

    print(f"Optimal c1: {x[0]:.4f}")
    print(f"Optimal c2: {x[1]:.4f}")
    print(f"Shadow Price (lambda): {x[2]:.4f}")

docs.text:
These relations are collected from the derivations above as a review map. Their assumptions and derivations remain part of the result; this box is not a substitute for them.

1. Core relation

\[f(x+h) - f(x-h) = 2hf'(x) + \frac{h^3}{3}f'''(x) + \dots\]

2. Core relation

\[\frac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h} = f'(x) + \frac{h^2}{6}f'''(x) + \dots\]

3. Core relation

\[4D(h/2) - D(h) \approx 3f'(x)\]

4. Core relation

\[D_{richardson} = \frac{4D(h/2) - D(h)}{3} = f'(x) + O(h^4)\]

Dimension notes: all quantities are scalars: \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), step \(h > 0\), and each estimate \(D(h) \approx f'(x) \in \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Key Takeaways: * Finite Differences: Good for quick checks or when you don't have the source code (black box functions). Use Central Difference. * Automatic Differentiation (JAX): The gold standard for modern economic modeling. It gives exact derivatives, is differentiable itself (Hessians!), and runs on GPUs. * Optimization: Combining Newton's Method with AD allows us to solve complex equilibria robustly.

docs.title: 1. Conceptual: Richardson Extrapolation
docs.text: The central difference has error \(O(h^2)\). Richardson extrapolation combines two central difference estimates (one with step \(h\), one with \(h/2\)) to cancel the \(h^2\) error term, resulting in \(O(h^4)\) accuracy. Derive the formula and implement it.

docs.title: 2. Applied: Batch MLE with vmap
docs.text: Use JAX to perform Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a linear regression model \(y = X\beta + \epsilon\). Write the likelihood function for a single observation, then use vmap to compute the total likelihood over a dataset. Use grad to find the \(\beta\) that maximizes likelihood.

docs.title: 3. Challenge: Second-Order Risk Aversion
docs.text:
For a CRRA utility function \(u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}\), use JAX to compute the Arrow-Pratt coefficient of relative risk aversion \(R(c) = -\frac{c u''(c)}{u'(c)}\). Verify numerically that it equals \(\gamma\) for any \(c\).

Failure analysis (Challenge): A central-difference derivative loses accuracy as \(h\) shrinks below \(10^{-5}\), contradicting the \(O(h^2)\) theory. Diagnose the rounding-vs-truncation trade-off, locate the optimal \(h \approx \varepsilon^{1/3}\) empirically, and plot total error against \(h\) with both regimes annotated.

docs.title: 04 Root Finding
docs.text:
Source notebook: 02-Numerical-Methods/04_Root_Finding.ipynb

Notebook outputs are intentionally omitted from the documentation build; code and narrative remain source-faithful.

docs.title: The Lens: Equilibrium is a Zero
docs.text:
What problem are we solving? In economics, equilibrium is defined by balance. * Market Clearing: Supply equals Demand \(\implies S(p) - D(p) = 0\). * Arbitrage: Returns are equalized \(\implies R_A - R_B = 0\). * Steady State: Capital doesn't change \(\implies s f(k) - \delta k = 0\).

These are all root-finding problems. We are looking for the variable \(x\) such that \(f(x) = 0\).

Why this method? Analytical solutions (\(x = \frac{-b \pm \dots}{2a}\)) are rare. We need numerical algorithms that can hunt down the zero for any function. * Bisection: Slow but guaranteed. Good for 1D problems where you know the bounds. * Newton-Raphson: Fast but risky. Requires derivatives. * Brent's Method: The industrial standard (hybrid). Safest for 1D. * Homotopy Continuation: A robust method for difficult systems of equations.

Economic question. In 04 Root Finding, what must remain economically invariant when the computational representation changes? In economic computation, an algorithm is part of the model: convergence tolerances, conditioning, discretization, and stopping rules can alter the apparent equilibrium. The central question is therefore not merely whether a routine returns a number, but whether that number is stable under tighter tolerances, alternative initial conditions, and an independent method. Treat every numerical result as an approximation with a measurable error budget.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this notebook, you will be able to: 1. Formulate economic equilibrium problems as root-finding tasks. 2. Apply the Fixed Point Iteration method and understand the Contraction Mapping Theorem. 3. Implement Bisection and Newton's method. 4. Solve for market clearing prices in a General Equilibrium model. 5. Utilize Homotopy Continuation to solve systems where Newton's method fails.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• 02-Numerical-Methods/03_Numerical_Differentiation.ipynb: Newton's method relies on derivatives.

Historical Context — Newton 1669, Raphson 1690. Isaac Newton described the iterative root method in manuscripts of 1669–1671 (solving a cubic near zero), and Joseph Raphson simplified it algebraically in 1690 — hence hyphenation that credits both. Thomas Simpson generalized it to higher dimensions in 1740; Brent's 1973 hybrid finally made it safe for production use.

Learning path: Building on 03_Numerical_Differentiation.ipynb; next continue with 05_Optimization.ipynb.

docs.title: Interactive Lab: Market-Clearing Root

Use the demand intercept to shift the market and watch the equilibrium price move. The point is not the widget itself: it makes the mapping from \(f(p)=Q_d(p)-Q_s(p)\) to an equilibrium price visible.

try:
    from ipywidgets import FloatSlider, interact

    @interact(demand_intercept=FloatSlider(value=12.0, min=6.0, max=20.0, step=0.5, description="Demand a"))
    def market_clearing_widget(demand_intercept=12.0):
        demand_slope, supply_intercept, supply_slope = 1.2, 1.0, 0.8
        root = (demand_intercept - supply_intercept) / (demand_slope + supply_slope)
        residual = demand_intercept - demand_slope * root - (supply_intercept + supply_slope * root)
        print(f"Equilibrium price = {root:.3f}; excess-demand residual = {residual:.2e}")
except ImportError:
    print("Install ipywidgets to use the market-clearing slider.")
