docs.title: 1. Theoretical Foundations: Exchange, Efficiency, and Existence
docs.text:
Before computing equilibria numerically, we establish what we are computing and why it is worth computing. Three questions organize the classical theory, and each has a precise answer:

  1. What is an equilibrium allocation, and what makes it "efficient"? → the Edgeworth box and the contract curve.
  2. Is the market outcome socially good? → the First and Second Welfare Theorems.
  3. Does an equilibrium even exist? → Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.

The third question is not pedantic: the numerical solvers used later in this notebook search for a price vector that clears all markets. If no such vector existed, the solver would be chasing a ghost, and its failure to converge would tell us nothing about our code.

docs.title: 1.1 The Edgeworth Box and the Contract Curve
docs.text:
Consider the simplest possible general-equilibrium economy: two agents (\(A\) and \(B\)), two goods (\(x\) and \(y\)), no production, and fixed total endowments \(\bar{x}, \bar{y}\). Because every unit not consumed by \(A\) must be consumed by \(B\), an allocation is fully described by \(A\)'s bundle alone: \((x_B, y_B) = (\bar{x} - x_A,\; \bar{y} - y_A)\).

This is what makes the Edgeworth box possible: a rectangle of width \(\bar{x}\) and height \(\bar{y}\) in which every point is a complete allocation of the whole economy. Agent \(A\)'s consumption is measured from the bottom-left origin, agent \(B\)'s from the top-right origin — reading \(B\)'s axes upside-down. \(A\)'s indifference curves bow outward from the lower-left; \(B\)'s bow outward from the upper-right.

Definition (Pareto efficiency). An allocation is Pareto efficient if no reallocation can make one agent better off without making the other worse off.

Geometrically, an allocation is Pareto efficient exactly when the two agents' indifference curves are tangent. If they merely cross, they carve out a lens-shaped region of allocations that both agents strictly prefer — so a mutually beneficial trade is available and the allocation was not efficient. Tangency is equivalent to equality of the marginal rates of substitution:

\[ MRS_A \;=\; \frac{\partial u_A/\partial x}{\partial u_A/\partial y} \;=\; \frac{\partial u_B/\partial x}{\partial u_B/\partial y} \;=\; MRS_B. \]

Definition (Contract curve). The contract curve is the locus of all Pareto-efficient allocations in the box — the set of tangency points, running from \(A\)'s origin to \(B\)'s origin.

Worked example (used in the code below). With Cobb-Douglas preferences \(u_A = x^{\alpha_A} y^{1-\alpha_A}\) and \(u_B = x^{\alpha_B} y^{1-\alpha_B}\), the marginal rate of substitution has the closed form

\[ MRS = \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\cdot\frac{y}{x}. \]

Setting \(MRS_A = MRS_B\) with \(k_i \equiv \alpha_i/(1-\alpha_i)\) and substituting \(B\)'s consumption:

\[ k_A \frac{y_A}{x_A} = k_B \frac{\bar{y} - y_A}{\bar{x} - x_A} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; k_A\, y_A (\bar{x} - x_A) = k_B\, (\bar{y} - y_A)\, x_A. \]

Collecting the \(y_A\) terms gives the contract curve in closed form:

\[ y_A(x_A) \;=\; \frac{k_B\, \bar{y}\, x_A}{k_A(\bar{x} - x_A) + k_B\, x_A}. \]

This is exactly the contract_curve_y function in the code cell below — the curve is not sketched by hand, it is computed from the tangency condition.

docs.title: 1.2 Walrasian Equilibrium
docs.text:
A Walrasian (competitive) equilibrium is a price vector \(p^* = (p_x, p_y)\) and an allocation such that (i) each agent demands the bundle maximizing utility subject to their budget constraint, evaluated at their endowment's market value, and (ii) all markets clear.

Only relative prices matter: scaling all prices by \(\lambda > 0\) scales every budget constraint by \(\lambda\) and leaves demands unchanged (demand functions are homogeneous of degree zero in prices). We therefore normalize by choosing a numeraire — below, \(p_y \equiv 1\).

Walras' Law. At any price vector, the value of aggregate excess demand is identically zero: \(p \cdot z(p) = 0\), where \(z(p)\) is the vector of excess demands.

Proof. Each agent's budget constraint binds when preferences are locally non-satiated: \(p \cdot (\text{demand}_i) = p \cdot (\text{endowment}_i)\), i.e. the value of each agent's excess demand is zero. Summing over agents gives \(p \cdot z(p) = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

The practical payoff: with \(N\) markets, if \(N-1\) clear then the \(N\)-th clears automatically (since \(p\cdot z = 0\) and the first \(N-1\) components of \(z\) vanish, the \(N\)-th must too, provided \(p_N \neq 0\)). This is why the solvers below search over \(N-1\) prices, not \(N\) — the system would otherwise be redundant and the Jacobian singular.

docs.title: 1.3 The Two Fundamental Welfare Theorems
docs.text:
First Fundamental Welfare Theorem. If preferences are locally non-satiated, then every Walrasian equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient.

Proof (by contradiction). Suppose the equilibrium allocation \(\{c_i^*\}\) at prices \(p^*\) is not efficient: there is a feasible allocation \(\{\hat{c}_i\}\) that every agent weakly prefers and at least one strictly prefers. For the agent who strictly prefers \(\hat{c}_i\): since \(c_i^*\) was chosen as the best affordable bundle, \(\hat{c}_i\) must have been unaffordable, so \(p^* \cdot \hat{c}_i > p^* \cdot e_i\) (where \(e_i\) is the endowment). For any agent who is merely weakly better off, local non-satiation gives \(p^* \cdot \hat{c}_i \ge p^* \cdot e_i\) — if \(\hat{c}_i\) were strictly cheaper, some bundle arbitrarily near \(\hat{c}_i\) would be both affordable and strictly better than \(c_i^*\), contradicting optimality of \(c_i^*\). Summing over all agents, the strict inequality survives:

\[ p^* \cdot \sum_i \hat{c}_i \;>\; p^* \cdot \sum_i e_i. \]

But \(\{\hat{c}_i\}\) was assumed feasible, meaning \(\sum_i \hat{c}_i = \sum_i e_i\), which forces the two sides to be equal — a contradiction. \(\blacksquare\)

Notice how little the theorem assumes: no convexity, no differentiability, only local non-satiation. Notice also what it does not say — nothing about fairness. An equilibrium in which one agent owns everything is Pareto efficient.

Second Fundamental Welfare Theorem. If preferences are additionally convex (and continuous, non-satiated), then any Pareto-efficient allocation can be achieved as a Walrasian equilibrium after a suitable lump-sum redistribution of endowments.

Proof sketch. Fix a Pareto-efficient allocation \(\{c_i^*\}\). For each agent, form the set of bundles strictly preferred to \(c_i^*\); convexity of preferences makes each such set convex, hence so is their aggregate sum \(V\). Efficiency means \(V\) does not intersect the set of feasible aggregate bundles. Two disjoint convex sets can be separated: the separating hyperplane theorem (proved in Appendix/A1-Real-Analysis.ipynb) supplies a nonzero price vector \(p^*\) such that everything in \(V\) costs at least as much as the aggregate endowment. That \(p^*\) is precisely a supporting price system: give each agent an endowment worth \(p^* \cdot c_i^*\), and \(c_i^*\) becomes their utility-maximizing choice. \(\blacksquare\)

Why convexity is indispensable here (but not for the First Theorem). With a non-convex preferred set, no hyperplane can separate it from the feasible set without cutting through — the tangency price would tempt the agent to jump to a distant bundle on the far side of the "dent" rather than stay put. Economically, the Second Theorem is the formal statement that efficiency and distribution are separable concerns: society can choose any efficient point it considers fair and decentralize it through markets, provided redistribution is lump-sum. The caveat is severe in practice, since real-world taxes distort behavior at the margin and are therefore not lump-sum.

docs.title: 1.4 Existence: Brouwer's Fixed-Point Theorem
docs.text:
Nothing so far guarantees an equilibrium price vector exists. This is the deepest result of the three, and the argument is beautiful: turn "market clearing" into "having a fixed point."

Brouwer's Fixed-Point Theorem. Every continuous function \(f : K \to K\) mapping a non-empty, compact, convex set \(K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) into itself has at least one fixed point: some \(p\) with \(f(p) = p\).

Applying it to markets. Because demands are homogeneous of degree zero, we can restrict prices to the unit simplex \(\Delta = \{ p \in \mathbb{R}^n_{+} : \sum_j p_j = 1 \}\), which is non-empty, compact, and convex — exactly Brouwer's hypotheses. Now define the price-adjustment map (Gale-Nikaido), which raises the relative price of any good in excess demand:

\[ f_j(p) \;=\; \frac{p_j + \max\{0,\, z_j(p)\}}{1 + \sum_{k} \max\{0,\, z_k(p)\}}, \qquad j = 1, \ldots, n. \]

The denominator renormalizes so that \(f(p)\) stays in \(\Delta\). If the excess demand function \(z\) is continuous, so is \(f\), and Brouwer applies: a fixed point \(p^*\) exists.

Why a fixed point is an equilibrium. At a fixed point, \(p_j^* = f_j(p^*)\) for every \(j\). Write \(\mu = \sum_k \max\{0, z_k(p^*)\} \ge 0\); the fixed-point condition rearranges to \(p_j^*\, \mu = \max\{0,\, z_j(p^*)\}\) for all \(j\). Multiply by \(z_j(p^*)\) and sum over \(j\):

\[ \mu \underbrace{\sum_j p_j^* z_j(p^*)}_{= \,0 \text{ by Walras' Law}} \;=\; \sum_j z_j(p^*) \max\{0,\, z_j(p^*)\} \;=\; \sum_j \big[\max\{0,\, z_j(p^*)\}\big]^2 . \]

The left side is zero by Walras' Law. The right side is a sum of squares, so every term must vanish: \(\max\{0, z_j(p^*)\} = 0\) for all \(j\), i.e. \(z_j(p^*) \le 0\) for every good — no good is in excess demand. Combined with Walras' Law and positive prices, this gives \(z_j(p^*) = 0\): all markets clear. \(\blacksquare\)

What the existence proof demands, and what it costs us. Continuity of \(z\) requires preferences to be continuous and convex (with non-convexities, demand jumps discontinuously as a price crosses a threshold and the fixed point can evaporate). Note also what the theorem does not deliver: uniqueness. Multiple equilibria are entirely possible, which is why the numerical solvers below can converge to different answers from different starting guesses — and why reporting the starting point matters when publishing CGE results.

With existence, efficiency, and decentralization settled, we can turn to actually computing equilibria.

# --- The Edgeworth Box: Equilibrium and the Contract Curve ---
# A two-agent, two-good pure exchange economy with Cobb-Douglas preferences,
# u_i(x, y) = x^alpha_i * y^(1 - alpha_i). Good Y is the numeraire (p_y = 1).

TOTAL_X, TOTAL_Y = 10.0, 10.0          # Aggregate endowments (box dimensions)
ALPHA_A, ALPHA_B = 0.6, 0.3            # Cobb-Douglas expenditure share on good X
ENDOW_A = np.array([8.0, 2.0])         # Agent A starts X-rich, Y-poor
ENDOW_B = np.array([TOTAL_X, TOTAL_Y]) - ENDOW_A


def utility(bundle: np.ndarray, alpha: float) -> float:
    """Cobb-Douglas utility u = x^alpha * y^(1-alpha)."""
    x, y = bundle
    return x**alpha * y ** (1 - alpha)


def demand(alpha: float, endowment: np.ndarray, prices: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Cobb-Douglas demand: spend fraction alpha of wealth on X, the rest on Y."""
    wealth = prices @ endowment
    return np.array([alpha * wealth / prices[0], (1 - alpha) * wealth / prices[1]])


def excess_demand_x(price_x: float) -> float:
    """Aggregate excess demand for good X. By Walras' Law, zeroing this
    clears the Y market automatically -- so we solve ONE equation, not two."""
    prices = np.array([price_x, 1.0])
    total_demand = (demand(ALPHA_A, ENDOW_A, prices)[0]
                    + demand(ALPHA_B, ENDOW_B, prices)[0])
    return total_demand - TOTAL_X


def contract_curve_y(x_a: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Pareto-efficient y_A as a function of x_A, from MRS_A = MRS_B.
    Derived in section 1.1: y_A = k_B * Ybar * x_A / (k_A(Xbar - x_A) + k_B x_A)."""
    k_a = ALPHA_A / (1 - ALPHA_A)
    k_b = ALPHA_B / (1 - ALPHA_B)
    return k_b * TOTAL_Y * x_a / (k_a * (TOTAL_X - x_a) + k_b * x_a)


# --- Solve for the Walrasian equilibrium price ---
# Closed form: setting excess demand to zero and solving the linear equation in p_x.
price_x_analytic = (ALPHA_A * ENDOW_A[1] + ALPHA_B * ENDOW_B[1]) / (
    TOTAL_X - ALPHA_A * ENDOW_A[0] - ALPHA_B * ENDOW_B[0]
)
price_x_star = brentq(excess_demand_x, 1e-6, 1e3)   # numerical confirmation
assert np.isclose(price_x_star, price_x_analytic), "closed form must match the solver"

prices_star = np.array([price_x_star, 1.0])
alloc_a = demand(ALPHA_A, ENDOW_A, prices_star)
alloc_b = demand(ALPHA_B, ENDOW_B, prices_star)

# --- Verify the theory numerically ---
# 1. Both markets clear (Walras' Law: we only imposed the X market).
assert np.isclose(alloc_a[0] + alloc_b[0], TOTAL_X), "X market must clear"
assert np.isclose(alloc_a[1] + alloc_b[1], TOTAL_Y), "Y market clears by Walras' Law"
# 2. First Welfare Theorem: the equilibrium allocation must be Pareto efficient,
#    i.e. it must lie exactly on the contract curve.
assert np.isclose(contract_curve_y(alloc_a[0]), alloc_a[1]), \
    "equilibrium must be Pareto efficient (First Welfare Theorem)"

# --- Plot the Edgeworth box ---
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))

x_grid = np.linspace(0.05, TOTAL_X - 0.05, 400)

# Indifference curves through the equilibrium allocation, for both agents.
u_a_star, u_b_star = utility(alloc_a, ALPHA_A), utility(alloc_b, ALPHA_B)
# For A: u = x^a y^(1-a)  =>  y = (u / x^a)^(1/(1-a))
y_a_star = (u_a_star / x_grid**ALPHA_A) ** (1 / (1 - ALPHA_A))
# For B, measured from the top-right origin: x_B = Xbar - x_A, y_B = Ybar - y_A
x_b_grid = TOTAL_X - x_grid
y_b_star = TOTAL_Y - (u_b_star / x_b_grid**ALPHA_B) ** (1 / (1 - ALPHA_B))

ax.plot(x_grid, y_a_star, color='tab:blue', lw=2,
        label="A's indifference curve through equilibrium")
ax.plot(x_grid, y_b_star, color='tab:red', lw=2,
        label="B's indifference curve through equilibrium")
ax.plot(x_grid, contract_curve_y(x_grid), color='black', lw=2.5, ls='--',
        label='Contract curve (Pareto set)')

# Budget line through the endowment with slope -p_x / p_y.
budget_y = ENDOW_A[1] + price_x_star * (ENDOW_A[0] - x_grid)
inside = (budget_y >= 0) & (budget_y <= TOTAL_Y)
ax.plot(x_grid[inside], budget_y[inside], color='tab:green', lw=1.8, alpha=0.9,
        label=f'Budget line (slope $-p_x/p_y = -{price_x_star:.3f}$)')

ax.plot(*ENDOW_A, 'o', color='tab:orange', ms=12, zorder=5,
        label=f'Endowment  ({ENDOW_A[0]:.1f}, {ENDOW_A[1]:.1f})')
ax.plot(*alloc_a, '*', color='black', ms=20, zorder=5,
        label=f'Equilibrium  ({alloc_a[0]:.2f}, {alloc_a[1]:.2f})')

ax.set_xlim(0, TOTAL_X)
ax.set_ylim(0, TOTAL_Y)
ax.set_xlabel("Good X  →  (Agent A)")
ax.set_ylabel("Good Y  →  (Agent A)")
ax.set_title('The Edgeworth Box: Trade from Endowment to Equilibrium',
             fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')

# Mirrored axes so agent B's consumption can be read from the top-right origin.
ax_b = ax.secondary_xaxis('top', functions=(lambda v: TOTAL_X - v, lambda v: TOTAL_X - v))
ax_b.set_xlabel("(Agent B)  ←  Good X")
ay_b = ax.secondary_yaxis('right', functions=(lambda v: TOTAL_Y - v, lambda v: TOTAL_Y - v))
ay_b.set_ylabel("(Agent B)  ←  Good Y")

ax.legend(loc='lower left', fontsize=9, framealpha=0.95)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

display(Markdown(
    f"> **Equilibrium price** $p_x/p_y = {price_x_star:.4f}$. "
    f"Agent A trades from the endowment $({ENDOW_A[0]:.1f}, {ENDOW_A[1]:.1f})$ to "
    f"$({alloc_a[0]:.2f}, {alloc_a[1]:.2f})$, selling X to buy Y.\n\n"
    f"> The equilibrium star sits **exactly on the contract curve** (asserted above), "
    f"and the two indifference curves are **tangent** there — the First Welfare "
    f"Theorem, verified numerically rather than merely asserted."
))

docs.title: 2. The Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) Framework
docs.text: We consider a closed economy with: - Two Factors: Labor (\(L\)) and Capital (\(K\)). - Two Sectors: Manufacturing (\(X\)) and Agriculture (\(Y\)). - Households: Own the factors and consume the goods.

docs.title: 2.1 The Model Equations
docs.text:
An equilibrium is a vector of prices \((P_X, P_Y, W, R)\) such that:

  1. Zero Profit Conditions: Price equals unit cost. $$ P_X = c_X(W, R), \quad P_Y = c_Y(W, R) $$ assuming Cobb-Douglas technologies: \(Y_i = A_i K_i^{\alpha_i} L_i^{1-\alpha_i}\).

  2. Market Clearing (Goods): Supply equals Demand. $$ Y_X = D_X(P_X, P_Y, I), \quad Y_Y = D_Y(P_X, P_Y, I) $$ where \(I = W L_{bar} + R K_{bar}\) is total income.

  3. Market Clearing (Factors): $$ L_X + L_Y = L_{bar}, \quad K_X + K_Y = K_{bar} $$

By Walras' Law, if \(N-1\) markets clear, the \(N^{th}\) market clears automatically. We normalize one price (numeraire), usually \(W=1\).

class CGEModel:
    """
    A 2-Sector (X, Y), 2-Factor (L, K) General Equilibrium Model.
    Technology: Cobb-Douglas.
    Preferences: Cobb-Douglas.
    """
    def __init__(self, L_bar=100, K_bar=50, alpha_X=0.3, alpha_Y=0.7, beta_c=0.5, A_X=1.0, A_Y=1.0):
        # Endowments
        self.L_bar = L_bar
        self.K_bar = K_bar
        # Technology: Y = A * K^alpha * L^(1-alpha)
        # Note: alpha here is Capital share (standard notation), usually labor is 1-alpha.
        # Let's clarify: alpha_X is Capital share in X.
        self.alpha_X = alpha_X
        self.alpha_Y = alpha_Y
        self.A_X = A_X
        self.A_Y = A_Y
        # Preferences: U = X^beta * Y^(1-beta)
        self.beta_c = beta_c

    def unit_cost(self, W, R, sector):
        """Calculates unit cost using the dual cost function for Cobb-Douglas."""
        if sector == 'X':
            alpha, A = self.alpha_X, self.A_X
        else:
            alpha, A = self.alpha_Y, self.A_Y

        # Cost function c(w,r) = (1/A) * (r/alpha)^alpha * (w/(1-alpha))^(1-alpha)
        cost = (1/A) * ((R/alpha)**alpha) * ((W/(1-alpha))**(1-alpha))
        return cost

    def factor_demands_per_unit(self, W, R, sector):
        """Shephard's Lemma: dC/dw = L/Y, dC/dr = K/Y"""
        # For CD: w*L = (1-alpha)*C*Y => L/Y = (1-alpha)*C/w
        unit_c = self.unit_cost(W, R, sector)
        if sector == 'X':
            alpha = self.alpha_X
        else:
            alpha = self.alpha_Y

        l_unit = (1 - alpha) * unit_c / W
        k_unit = alpha * unit_c / R
        return l_unit, k_unit

    def excess_demand_system(self, vars):
        """
        System of equations to solve for equilibrium prices.
        Unknowns: vars = [P_X, P_Y, R] (Numeraire W=1)
        Equations: 
        1. P_X = UnitCost_X
        2. P_Y = UnitCost_Y
        3. Labor Market Clearing (or Capital)
        """
        P_X, P_Y, R = vars
        W = 1.0 # Numeraire

        # 1. Zero Profit Conditions
        cost_X = self.unit_cost(W, R, 'X')
        cost_Y = self.unit_cost(W, R, 'Y')
        eq1 = P_X - cost_X
        eq2 = P_Y - cost_Y

        # 2. Demand Side
        Income = W * self.L_bar + R * self.K_bar
        D_X = self.beta_c * Income / P_X
        D_Y = (1 - self.beta_c) * Income / P_Y

        # 3. Factor Demand
        lx, kx = self.factor_demands_per_unit(W, R, 'X')
        ly, ky = self.factor_demands_per_unit(W, R, 'Y')

        # Total Factor Demand
        L_demand = lx * D_X + ly * D_Y
        K_demand = kx * D_X + ky * D_Y

        # 4. Market Clearing Errors
        eq3 = self.L_bar - L_demand
        # eq4 = self.K_bar - K_demand # Redundant by Walras Law

        return [eq1, eq2, eq3]

    def solve_autarky(self):
        """Finds the autarky equilibrium."""
        # Initial guess: Prices approx 1, R approx 1
        guess = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
        sol = root(self.excess_demand_system, guess, method='lm')

        if not sol.success:
            print("Warning: Solver failed to converge.")

        self.P_X, self.P_Y, self.R = sol.x
        self.W = 1.0
        return pd.Series({'P_X': self.P_X, 'P_Y': self.P_Y, 'W': self.W, 'R': self.R})

    def get_excess_demand_goods(self, P_X, P_Y):
        """
        Calculates excess demand for goods X and Y given WORLD prices.
        To do this, we must solve for internal factor prices W, R consistent with these goods prices.
        """
        # Given P_X, P_Y, we need to find W, R that satisfy zero profit.
        # P_X = c_X(W, R)
        # P_Y = c_Y(W, R)
        # This is a 2x2 system for factor prices. (Stolper-Samuelson mapping)

        def factor_price_sys(vars):
            W, R = vars
            return [self.unit_cost(W, R, 'X') - P_X,
                    self.unit_cost(W, R, 'Y') - P_Y]

        try:
            f_sol = root(factor_price_sys, [1.0, 1.0], method='lm')
            if not f_sol.success:
                warnings.warn(f"Factor price solver did not converge for P_X={P_X:.4f}, P_Y={P_Y:.4f}")
            W, R = f_sol.x
        except (ValueError, RuntimeError) as e:
            warnings.warn(f"Factor price solver failed for P_X={P_X:.4f}, P_Y={P_Y:.4f}: {e}")
            return np.array([np.nan, np.nan])

        # Now calculate supply and demand at these factor prices
        # Supply is determined by factor endowments and optimal K/L ratios.
        lx, kx = self.factor_demands_per_unit(W, R, 'X')
        ly, ky = self.factor_demands_per_unit(W, R, 'Y')

        # Solve linear system for outputs Y_X, Y_Y:
        # lx * Y_X + ly * Y_Y = L_bar
        # kx * Y_X + ky * Y_Y = K_bar
        A_mat = np.array([[lx, ly], [kx, ky]])
        b_vec = np.array([self.L_bar, self.K_bar])
        try:
            outputs = np.linalg.solve(A_mat, b_vec)
            Y_X, Y_Y = outputs
        except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
             # Outside Cone of Diversification (specialization)
             warnings.warn(f"Singular factor demand matrix at P_X={P_X:.4f}, P_Y={P_Y:.4f}. Outside cone of diversification.")
             return np.array([0.0, 0.0])

        # Demand
        Income = W * self.L_bar + R * self.K_bar
        D_X = self.beta_c * Income / P_X
        D_Y = (1 - self.beta_c) * Income / P_Y

        return np.array([D_X - Y_X, D_Y - Y_Y])

# --- Instantiate and Solve for Autarky ---
usa = CGEModel(L_bar=100, K_bar=100, alpha_X=0.3, alpha_Y=0.7) # Balanced
res = usa.solve_autarky()

print("> **Note:** Autarky Equilibrium Found:")
display(res.to_frame('Value'))

docs.title: 3. The Heckscher-Ohlin Model of Trade
docs.text:
We now introduce a second country. - Home: Labor Abundant (\(L=100, K=50\)). - Foreign: Capital Abundant (\(L=50, K=100\)). - Technology: Identical in both countries.

Heckscher-Ohlin Theorem: A country will export the good that uses its abundant factor intensively. - Sector X is Labor Intensive (\(\alpha_X=0.3\) is capital share, so labor share is 0.7). - Sector Y is Capital Intensive (\(\alpha_Y=0.7\) is capital share).

Prediction: Home (Labor abundant) should export X (Labor intensive).

class HeckscherOhlinSystem:
    def __init__(self, home_model, foreign_model):
        self.home = home_model
        self.foreign = foreign_model

    def world_excess_demand(self, prices):
        # We solve for relative price P = P_X / P_Y
        # Let P_Y = 1 (Numeraire for world trade)
        P_X = prices[0]
        P_Y = 1.0

        ed_home = self.home.get_excess_demand_goods(P_X, P_Y)
        ed_fgn = self.foreign.get_excess_demand_goods(P_X, P_Y)

        # Return global excess demand for X (Walras Law handles Y)
        return ed_home[0] + ed_fgn[0]

# Setup Countries
home = CGEModel(L_bar=100, K_bar=50, alpha_X=0.3, alpha_Y=0.7)  # Labor Rich
foreign = CGEModel(L_bar=50, K_bar=100, alpha_X=0.3, alpha_Y=0.7) # Capital Rich

# 1. Check Autarky Prices
p_home = home.solve_autarky()
p_fgn = foreign.solve_autarky()
rel_p_home = p_home['P_X'] / p_home['P_Y']
rel_p_fgn = p_fgn['P_X'] / p_fgn['P_Y']

print(f"> **Note:** Autarky Relative Price (Px/Py): Home={rel_p_home:.3f}, Foreign={rel_p_fgn:.3f}")
print(f"> **Observation:** Good X is cheaper in Home ({rel_p_home:.3f} < {rel_p_fgn:.3f}), creating an incentive to export it.")

# 2. Solve for Free Trade Equilibrium
ho_sys = HeckscherOhlinSystem(home, foreign)

# Root finding for World Price P_X (fixing P_Y=1)
sol_trade = root(ho_sys.world_excess_demand, [1.0], method='lm')
world_Px = sol_trade.x[0]

print(f"\n> **Note:** World Equilibrium Price Px (Py=1): {world_Px:.3f}")

# 3. Analyze Trade Flows
ed_home_trade = home.get_excess_demand_goods(world_Px, 1.0)
ed_fgn_trade = foreign.get_excess_demand_goods(world_Px, 1.0)

print(f"> **Trade Flow:** Home Exports X: {-ed_home_trade[0]:.3f} units (Negative Excess Demand = Supply)")
print(f"> **Trade Flow:** Foreign Imports X: {ed_fgn_trade[0]:.3f} units")

docs.title: 3.1 Visualizing World Equilibrium
docs.text:
To better understand the solution, we plot the Global Excess Demand for Good X as a function of the relative price \(P_X\). The equilibrium is where this curve crosses zero.

# Define range of prices between autarky prices
p_min = min(rel_p_home, rel_p_fgn) * 0.9
p_max = max(rel_p_home, rel_p_fgn) * 1.1
prices = np.linspace(p_min, p_max, 50)
excess_demands = []

print("Calculating excess demand curve...")
for p in prices:
    ed = ho_sys.world_excess_demand([p])
    excess_demands.append(ed)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(prices, excess_demands, color='darkblue', linewidth=2, label='World Excess Demand (Good X)')
plt.axhline(0, color='black', linewidth=1)
plt.axvline(world_Px, color='red', linestyle='--', label=f'Equilibrium Price ({world_Px:.2f})')

# Mark Autarky Prices

plt.axvline(rel_p_fgn, color='orange', linestyle=':', alpha=0.7, label='Foreign Autarky Price')

1. Core relation

\[MRS_A \;=\; \frac{\partial u_A/\partial x}{\partial u_A/\partial y} \;=\; \frac{\partial u_B/\partial x}{\partial u_B/\partial y} \;=\; MRS_B.\]

\[k_A \frac{y_A}{x_A} = k_B \frac{\bar{y} - y_A}{\bar{x} - x_A} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; k_A\, y_A (\bar{x} - x_A) = k_B\, (\bar{y} - y_A)\, x_A.\]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this notebook, we moved from the abstract theory of the "invisible hand" to a concrete, computational implementation.

  1. CGE Modeling: We built a solver that finds the unique price vector clearing all markets simultaneously. This is the core algorithm used in policy institutions worldwide.
  2. Heckscher-Ohlin: We verified the classic trade theorem. The labor-abundant country had a lower autarky price for the labor-intensive good and became an exporter of that good under free trade.
  3. Gains from Trade: Trade equalized goods prices. While not explicitly shown here, this convergence typically benefits aggregate welfare, though it creates winners and losers (Stolper-Samuelson theorem) within each country.

This framework can be easily extended to \(N\) sectors and households, forming the basis of modern trade policy analysis.

docs.title: The Lens: Strategic Interaction
docs.text:
What problem are we solving? In perfect competition, agents are price takers; they don't care what others do. In Game Theory, agents are strategic: my optimal move depends on what I think you will do, and you are thinking the same about me. This framework is essential for analyzing oligopolies, bargaining, and auctions. Mechanism Design flips the problem: if we want a specific outcome (e.g., efficiency), what are the rules of the game (the auction format) that will lead self-interested agents to choose it?

Why this method? We solve for the Nash Equilibrium: a situation where no player wants to deviate given what others are doing. * Normal Form Games: Simultaneous moves (Prisoner's Dilemma). * Auctions: Bidding strategies in First-Price vs. Second-Price auctions. * Revenue Equivalence: A stunning result showing that different auction formats yield the same expected revenue.

Economic question. In 03 Game Theory and Auctions, what must remain economically invariant when the computational representation changes? Microeconomic computation makes equilibrium and incentive constraints operational. The useful question is how preferences, technologies, information, or strategic beliefs map into choices and welfare, and whether the computed solution respects feasibility, optimality, and equilibrium conditions. Whenever multiple equilibria or corner solutions are possible, the numerical method should expose rather than hide that economic structure.

docs.title: 1. The Complexity of Finding Nash Equilibria
docs.text:
While finding a Nash equilibrium in a simple 2x2 game is straightforward, the problem's difficulty scales poorly. The premier algorithm for finding at least one Nash equilibrium in a two-player game is the Lemke-Howson algorithm, which works by traversing the vertices of a geometric representation of the game's payoffs. However, its worst-case performance is exponential in the number of strategies.

This computational hardness was formalized in a landmark 2009 paper by Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou, who showed that finding a Nash equilibrium is PPAD-complete. PPAD (Polynomial Parity Arguments on Directed graphs) is a complexity class that captures problems where a solution is guaranteed to exist by a specific kind of non-constructive argument (e.g., "if a directed graph has an unbalanced node, it must have another one"), but finding that solution may be intractable. For economists, the implication is profound: if finding a Nash equilibrium is computationally hard, it's less plausible to assume that real-world agents in complex strategic settings will be able to find and play such an equilibrium. This motivates the search for alternative, more tractable solution concepts.

docs.title: Finding Nash Equilibria with nashpy

# Payoff matrix for a classic 2x2 game: "Battle of the Sexes"
payoffs_A = np.array([[3, 1], [0, 2]]) # Player A's payoffs (Opera, Football)
payoffs_B = np.array([[2, 1], [0, 3]]) # Player B's payoffs (Opera, Football)

    battle_of_sexes = nash.Game(payoffs_A, payoffs_B)
    # The support_enumeration method iterates through all possible subsets of strategies
    # to find all Nash equilibria for a two-player game. This is feasible for small games.
    equilibria = list(battle_of_sexes.support_enumeration())
    display(Markdown(f'> **Note:** Found {len(equilibria)} Nash Equilibria for Battle of the Sexes:'))
    for i, eq in enumerate(equilibria):
        print(f"  Eq {i+1} (A's mix, B's mix): ({np.round(eq[0], 2)}, {np.round(eq[1], 2)})")
else:
    print("nashpy is not installed - skipping support enumeration "
          "(pip install nashpy to run this cell).")

Note: The first two are pure strategy equilibria (Opera,Opera and Football,Football). The third is the mixed strategy equilibrium where players randomize to make their opponent indifferent.

# Intersections

docs.title: 1.1 Beyond Nash: Correlated Equilibrium
docs.text:
Given the difficulty of computing and selecting among Nash equilibria, a more general and computationally tractable concept is the Correlated Equilibrium (CE), introduced by Robert Aumann in 1974 (work for which he shared the 2005 Nobel Prize). The intuition is to introduce a trusted third party (a "correlating device" or a "traffic light") that privately recommends an action to each player. The recommendations are drawn from a joint probability distribution over all possible action profiles that is known to all players.

A distribution is a Correlated Equilibrium if, for every player, assuming all other players follow their recommendations, it is optimal for that player to also follow their recommendation. This is a weaker solution concept than Nash (every Nash equilibrium is also a CE), but it has a crucial advantage: the set of correlated equilibria forms a convex polytope defined by a set of linear inequalities. This means we can find a CE by using linear programming, which is computationally efficient (solvable in polynomial time).

docs.title: Finding a Correlated Equilibrium via Linear Programming
docs.text:
def find_ce(p1_payoffs, p2_payoffs):
    n1, n2 = p1_payoffs.shape
    # We want to maximize the sum of payoffs (social welfare)
    # linprog minimizes, so we use the negative of the sum of payoffs
    objective_coeffs = -(p1_payoffs + p2_payoffs).flatten()

    # Constraint: Probabilities must sum to 1
    A_eq = [np.ones(n1 * n2)]
    b_eq = [1]

    # Incentive compatibility constraints (A_ub * x <= b_ub)
    A_ub, b_ub = [], []

    # For player 1, for each action i, the incentive is that the expected payoff
    # of playing i is >= the expected payoff of deviating to i'
    # sum_j p(i,j) * u1(i,j) >= sum_j p(i,j) * u1(i',j)
    # This can be rewritten as: sum_j p(i,j) * (u1(i',j) - u1(i,j)) <= 0
    for i in range(n1):
        for i_prime in range(n1):
            if i == i_prime:
                continue
            constraint_row = np.zeros((n1, n2))
            for j in range(n2):
                constraint_row[i, j] = p1_payoffs[i_prime, j] - p1_payoffs[i, j]
            A_ub.append(constraint_row.flatten())
            b_ub.append(0)

    # Similar incentive constraints for player 2
    for j in range(n2):
        for j_prime in range(n2):
            if j == j_prime:
                continue
            constraint_row = np.zeros((n1, n2))
            for i in range(n1):
                constraint_row[i, j] = p2_payoffs[i, j_prime] - p2_payoffs[i, j]
            A_ub.append(constraint_row.flatten())
            b_ub.append(0)

    # Solve the linear program
    res = linprog(c=objective_coeffs, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub, A_eq=A_eq, b_eq=b_eq, bounds=(0, 1))

    if res.success:
        # The result is the correlated equilibrium distribution
        return res.x.reshape((n1, n2))
    else:
        print(f"Linear program failed to converge: {res.message}")
        return None

ce_dist = find_ce(payoffs_A, payoffs_B)
if ce_dist is not None:
    pass

Note: Found a correlated equilibrium distribution that maximizes total welfare:

if ce_dist is not None:
    # Round to handle small numerical precision issues
    df_ce = pd.DataFrame(np.round(ce_dist, 5), index=['A:Opera', 'A:Football'], columns=['B:Opera', 'B:Football'])
    print(df_ce)

Note: This CE puts a 0.5 probability on each of the pure-strategy Nash equilibria, achieving the highest possible total payoff of (2.5, 2.5). The 'traffic light' tells them to coordinate on one of the two good outcomes.

docs.title: 2. Mechanism Design: Engineering the Rules of the Game
docs.text:
If finding equilibria in a given game is hard, an even more interesting problem is inverse game theory, or mechanism design. Here, we assume the role of a social planner or platform owner. We know agents are self-interested, so we cannot simply dictate what they should do. Instead, we design the rules of the game (the mechanism) such that the equilibrium outcome of agents playing strategically achieves our desired objective.

A mechanism defines: 1. A set of allowed actions or messages agents can send (e.g., placing a bid). 2. An allocation rule that maps the set of all messages to an outcome (e.g., who gets an item). 3. A payment rule that maps the set of all messages to payments (e.g., how much the winner pays).

The goal is to design rules that satisfy certain properties, such as truthfulness (incentive compatibility), social welfare maximization, or revenue maximization.

docs.title: 2.1 Application: Sponsored Search Auctions
docs.text:
The market for sponsored search ads (the ads you see at the top of a Google search) is a triumph of mechanism design. Early online ad auctions were simple first-price auctions, which led to complex bidding behavior and unstable revenues. A key innovation was to move to a Generalized Second-Price (GSP) auction that also incorporated the ad's quality.

In a modern GSP-like auction: 1. Each advertiser has a Quality Score, an estimate of the ad's relevance and click-through rate, determined by the platform. 2. Advertisers are ranked by their AdRank = Bid × Quality Score. 3. The highest-ranked advertiser gets the first slot, the second-highest gets the second, and so on. 4. The price per click paid by the advertiser in slot \(j\) is the minimum bid they would have needed to keep their rank above advertiser \(j+1\). This is calculated as: Price_j = AdRank_{j+1} / QualityScore_j.

This system is not perfectly truthful, but it creates powerful incentives for advertisers not only to bid high but also to create high-quality, relevant ads. This alignment of incentives benefits the platform (more clicks), the users (more relevant ads), and the advertisers (higher quality ads are "cheaper").

docs.title: Simulating a Generalized Second-Price (GSP) Auction
docs.text:
def simulate_gsp(bids, quality_scores):
    ad_data = [{'name': f"Advertiser {i+1}", 'bid': bid, 'quality': quality} 
               for i, (bid, quality) in enumerate(zip(bids, quality_scores))]

    # Calculate AdRank for each advertiser
    for ad in ad_data:
        ad['adrank'] = ad['bid'] * ad['quality']

    # Sort advertisers by AdRank in descending order
    sorted_ads = sorted(ad_data, key=lambda item: item['adrank'], reverse=True)

    # Determine allocation and prices
    results = []
    for i, ad in enumerate(sorted_ads):
        # The price is determined by the AdRank of the advertiser below them
        next_adrank = sorted_ads[i+1]['adrank'] if i + 1 < len(sorted_ads) else 0
        price = next_adrank / ad['quality'] if ad['quality'] > 0 else 0
        results.append({'Winner': ad['name'], 'Slot': i + 1, 'AdRank': ad['adrank'],
                        'Bid': ad['bid'], 'Quality': ad['quality'], 'Price/Click': price})

    return pd.DataFrame(results).set_index('Slot')

# --- Simulation Parameters ---
advertiser_bids = [2.50, 3.10, 1.80, 2.80]
quality_scores  = [8,    5,    9,    7]

Note: Figure 1: GSP Auction Results

gsp_results = simulate_gsp(advertiser_bids, quality_scores)
print(gsp_results.round(2))

Note: Advertiser 1 wins the top slot with the highest AdRank (20.0). They pay a price per click of $2.45, determined by Advertiser 4's AdRank (19.6) divided by their own quality score (8). Note how Advertiser 3, despite a low bid, gets a good slot due to a high quality score.

docs.title: 2.2 The VCG Mechanism: Achieving Truthfulness and Efficiency
docs.text:
The Revelation Principle is a foundational result in mechanism design. It states that for any outcome achievable by some complex, indirect mechanism, there exists an equivalent direct-revelation mechanism that is truthful (incentive-compatible) and achieves the same outcome. This simplifies the design problem immensely: we can restrict our search to truthful mechanisms without loss of generality.

The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction is the canonical truthful mechanism for maximizing social welfare (the sum of all agents' values for the outcome). Its key payment rule is that each agent pays for the harm their presence causes to other agents. This is the social opportunity cost, or negative externality, they impose on the rest of society.

VCG Procedure: 1. Allocation: Collect bids (which, in equilibrium, will be agents' true values) and find the allocation of items that maximizes the total reported value for all agents (\(W^*\)). 2. Payment: For each winning agent \(i\), calculate the total value that all other agents would have received if agent \(i\) had not participated (\(W_{-i}^*\)). Agent \(i\) pays the difference between the welfare others would have gotten without them, and the welfare they actually got with them: Payment_i = \(W_{-i}^*\) - (Welfare of others in the actual allocation). This ensures that an agent's utility is exactly equal to the social surplus they create, aligning their private incentive with the social good.

docs.title: Simulating a VCG Auction for a Combinatorial Problem
docs.text:
def solve_combinatorial_auction(valuations):
    bidders = list(valuations.keys())
    if not bidders:
        return {}, 0
    items = sorted(list(set(item for b in bidders for bundle in valuations[b] for item in bundle)))

    best_welfare = -1
    best_alloc = None

    # Iterate through all possible assignments of items to bidders (or no one)
    for assignment in itertools.product(bidders + [None], repeat=len(items)):
        alloc = {b: [] for b in bidders}
        for item_idx, bidder in enumerate(assignment):
            if bidder is not None:
                alloc[bidder].append(items[item_idx])

        current_welfare = 0
        for b in bidders:
            bundle_str = "".join(sorted(alloc[b]))
            current_welfare += valuations[b].get(bundle_str, 0)

        if current_welfare > best_welfare:
            best_welfare = current_welfare
            best_alloc = {b: "".join(sorted(alloc[b])) or None for b in bidders}

    return best_alloc, best_welfare


def simulate_vcg(valuations):
    optimal_alloc, total_welfare = solve_combinatorial_auction(valuations)
    payments = {}
    for bidder in valuations:
        # Welfare of others in the optimal allocation
        welfare_of_others_with_bidder = sum(valuations[b].get(optimal_alloc[b], 0) for b in valuations if b != bidder)

        # What would welfare be without this bidder?
        valuations_without_bidder = {k: v for k, v in valuations.items() if k != bidder}
        alloc_without_bidder, welfare_without_bidder = solve_combinatorial_auction(valuations_without_bidder)

        # Payment is the harm caused to others
        payments[bidder] = welfare_without_bidder - welfare_of_others_with_bidder

    return optimal_alloc, payments

# Bidders have different values for individual items and the bundle 'XY'
bidder_valuations = {
    'Alice': {'X': 5, 'Y': 10, 'XY': 18}, # Values the bundle at a premium (complementary goods)
    'Bob':   {'X': 8, 'Y': 6,  'XY': 12}  # Values items more separately (substitute goods)
}

Note: Figure 2: VCG Combinatorial Auction Results

alloc, p = simulate_vcg(bidder_valuations)
print(f"Optimal allocation: {alloc}")
print(f"VCG Payments: {p}")

Note: Alice gets the bundle because her value of $18 is higher than Bob's standalone welfare without her, which is $12 — his declared value for the bundle 'XY'. (His separate values of \(8+\)6=14 cannot be combined by the mechanism, since he reported a bundle value of only $12.) Alice pays $12, which is exactly the value Bob would have gotten if she wasn't there. This is the 'harm' she does to Bob.

Common Pitfalls in This Lecture

  • One equilibrium is not the prediction. nashpy may return a single Nash equilibrium among several. With multiple equilibria, reporting one as 'the' outcome ignores selection — discuss refinements or payoffs before concluding.
  • Mixed strategies from purged supports. Computing mixed probabilities without first eliminating dominated strategies can put weight on actions no rational player uses, producing a 'solution' that fails its own support conditions. Verify each support action is a best response.

docs.title: 3. Exercises
docs.text:
1. Correlated vs. Nash: For the "Battle of the Sexes" game, is the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium also a correlated equilibrium? Show why or why not by checking if its probability distribution satisfies the incentive compatibility constraints for a CE. (Hint: A Nash equilibrium is always a CE, but it's useful to prove it for a specific case).

  2. GSP and Truthfulness: The GSP auction is not perfectly truthful. Using the simulation parameters from section 2.1, suppose Advertiser 1's true value per click is $3.00. Could they increase their profit by bidding something other than $2.50? (Profit = Clicks * (True Value - Price)). For simplicity, assume the number of clicks an ad in slot k gets is 100 / k. Calculate Advertiser 1's profit with their current bid, and then see if they can do better by bidding, say, $1.90 to drop to a lower slot with a much lower price.

  3. VCG Analysis: In our VCG simulation, what would happen if Alice's valuation for the bundle 'XY' was only $13? Rerun the simulation by changing the bidder_valuations dictionary and explain the new allocation and payments. Why is VCG robust to such changes in valuations, and how does it always ensure the socially efficient outcome?

  4. The Gale-Shapley Algorithm: The Gale-Shapley algorithm (1962) provides a method for finding a stable matching in a two-sided market (e.g., medical residents to hospitals, students to schools). Research the algorithm. Is it guaranteed to find a unique stable matching? Is it strategy-proof (truthful) for all participants? Explain which side of the market has an incentive to be truthful.

  5. Algorithmic Fairness: A growing area of concern is algorithmic fairness. In the context of the GSP auction, how might the use of a proprietary, black-box Quality Score lead to outcomes that are considered unfair or anti-competitive? For example, what if the Quality Score model inadvertently penalizes ads from new businesses or those using certain dialects of a language? What kind of data would you need to test for such biases?

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
• Best response: \(BR_i(a_{-i})=\arg\max_{a_i} u_i(a_i,a_{-i})\).
  • Nash equilibrium: \(a_i^*\in BR_i(a_{-i}^*)\) for every player \(i\).
  • Mixed equilibrium: each action in the support yields the same expected payoff.
  • First-price symmetric bidding: the equilibrium bid is obtained by trading off a higher winning probability against the lower surplus conditional on winning.
  • Revenue equivalence: under the standard independent-private-values assumptions, allocation-equivalent mechanisms with the same zero type yield the same expected revenue.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Strategic interaction fundamentally changes the nature of optimization.

Key Takeaways: * Nash Equilibrium: The central solution concept where beliefs and actions are consistent. * Subgame Perfection: In dynamic games, credible threats rule out time-inconsistent strategies. * Revenue Equivalence: Under certain conditions, different auction formats (First-Price, Second-Price) yield the same expected revenue for the seller.

docs.title: The Lens: Choosing Categories
docs.text:
What problem are we solving? Standard demand theory assumes we choose a continuous quantity (how much gas to buy). But many important decisions are discrete (which car to buy, which mode of transport to take). Discrete Choice Models provide the econometric framework for analyzing choices between mutually exclusive alternatives. The foundational assumption is the Random Utility Model (RUM): agents choose the option that gives the highest utility, but the econometrician only observes part of that utility.

Why this method? We model the probability of choosing an option. * Logit Model: Assumes error terms follow a Type I Extreme Value (Gumbel) distribution. This yields closed-form choice probabilities. * IIA Property: The ratio of probabilities for any two alternatives is independent of other alternatives (a restrictive but simplifying assumption).

Economic question. In 04 Discrete Choice Models, what must remain economically invariant when the computational representation changes? Microeconomic computation makes equilibrium and incentive constraints operational. The useful question is how preferences, technologies, information, or strategic beliefs map into choices and welfare, and whether the computed solution respects feasibility, optimality, and equilibrium conditions. Whenever multiple equilibria or corner solutions are possible, the numerical method should expose rather than hide that economic structure.

docs.title: 1. The Random Utility Model (RUM) Framework
docs.text:
The modern approach to discrete choice analysis was developed in the 1960s and 1970s, culminating in the work of Daniel McFadden, for which he received the 2000 Nobel Prize in Economics. The Random Utility Model (RUM) provides the theoretical foundation. It frames the choice problem from the perspective of an econometrician who has imperfect information about the decision-maker's utility.

The utility individual \(n\) derives from choosing alternative \(j\) is: $$ U_{nj} = V_{nj} + \epsilon_{nj} $$ Where \(V_{nj} = \mathbf{X}_{nj}'\beta\) is the systematic (observable) utility and \(\epsilon_{nj}\) is the stochastic (unobservable) utility. The probability that agent \(n\) chooses alternative \(i\) is the probability that its utility is the highest: $$ P_{ni} = \text{Prob}(V_{ni} + \epsilon_{ni} > V_{nj} + \epsilon_{nj} \quad \forall j \neq i) $$ The specific functional form of this probability depends entirely on the assumption made about the joint distribution of the error terms.

docs.title: 2.1 Derivation from Gumbel Distributed Errors
docs.text:
The Multinomial Logit (MNL) model arises from the assumption that the error terms \(\epsilon_{nj}\) are independently and identically distributed (IID) according to a Type I Extreme Value (Gumbel) distribution. The CDF of the Gumbel distribution is \(F(\epsilon) = \exp(-e^{-\epsilon})\).

This assumption is powerful because the difference of two Gumbel variables follows a logistic distribution, and the maximum of several Gumbel variables also has a known, simple distribution. This allows the complex integral for the choice probability to be solved analytically, yielding the famous logit formula: $$ P_{ni} = \frac{e^{V_{ni}}}{\sum_{j \in C_n} e^{V_{nj}}} $$

docs.title: 2.2 The IIA Property and its Limitations
docs.text:
The IID assumption leads to the Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives (IIA) property. The ratio of probabilities for any two alternatives, \(P_{ni}/P_{nk} = e^{V_{ni}}/e^{V_{nk}}\), depends only on the attributes of those two alternatives. This implies that introducing a new alternative reduces the probabilities of all existing alternatives proportionally.

The classic illustration of why this is a problem is the "red bus/blue bus" problem. Suppose a commuter can choose between a car and a blue bus, each with a 50% market share. The logit model would correctly predict this. Now, a new option is introduced: a red bus, identical to the blue bus in every way except color. Intuitively, the total share of bus travel should remain 50%, with the blue and red buses splitting it (25% each), and the car's share should be unchanged. However, the MNL model, due to the IIA property, would predict that the new red bus draws proportionally from the car and the blue bus, resulting in the car's share falling to 33.3%, and the blue and red buses each having a 33.3% share. This is clearly unrealistic and motivates the need for more advanced models that can handle correlations between alternatives.

docs.title: 3. Relaxing the IIA Assumption: Nested and Mixed Logit
3.1 The Nested Logit Model
docs.text:
The Nested Logit model partially relaxes the IIA assumption by grouping similar alternatives into "nests." The error term \(\epsilon_{nj}\) is decomposed into a component common to the nest and a component specific to the alternative. This induces correlation among alternatives within the same nest.

The choice probability becomes a product of the probability of choosing a nest and the probability of choosing an alternative within that nest: $$ P_{ni} = P(i | \text{nest } k) \times P(\text{nest } k) $$ The model estimates a nesting parameter, \(\lambda_k\), which measures the degree of correlation within the nest. If \(\lambda_k=1\), the model collapses to the standard MNL.

docs.title: Example: Estimating a Nested Logit Model with pylogit
docs.text:
try:
    import pylogit as pl
    PYLOGIT_AVAILABLE = True
except ImportError:
    PYLOGIT_AVAILABLE = False

if PYLOGIT_AVAILABLE:
    # Create a long-format dataset for a transport choice problem
    data = OrderedDict([
        ('mode_id', [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]),
        ('choice', [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0]),
        ('cost', [7, 8, 10, 7, 8, 10, 7, 8, 10]),
        ('time', [2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 2, 4, 6]),
        ('obs_id', [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3])
    ])
    df = pd.DataFrame(data)

    # Define the model specification and nests
    spec = OrderedDict([
        ('intercept', {1: 'const', 2: 'const', 3: 'const'}),
        ('cost', [[1, 2, 3], 'cost']),
        ('time', [[1, 2, 3], 'time'])
    ])
    # Nest Structure: 'private' (car=1) vs 'public' (bus=2, train=3)
    nests = OrderedDict([('private', [1]), ('public', [2, 3])])

    # Create and fit the model
    model = pl.create_choice_model(data=df, alt_id_col='mode_id', obs_id_col='obs_id',
                                   choice_col='choice', specification=spec, model_type='Nested Logit',
                                   names=OrderedDict([(1, 'Car'), (2, 'Bus'), (3, 'Train')]), nests=nests)
    model.fit_mle(np.zeros(len(spec) + len(nests) - 1))

    print(model.get_statsmodels_summary())

Note: The nesting parameter for the 'public' nest is estimated. If it is significantly different from 1, it indicates correlation between the bus and train alternatives, and the nested logit is a better fit than the standard MNL.

Note: Pylogit is not installed. Skipping Nested Logit example.

docs.title: 3.2 The Mixed Logit Model
docs.text:
The Mixed Logit (or Random Coefficients Logit) model is the most flexible and widely used discrete choice model. It fully overcomes the IIA property by allowing the coefficients (\(\ eta\)) themselves to be random, varying across individuals according to a specified distribution (e.g., price sensitivity \(\beta_{price}\) is normally distributed in the population).

The utility function becomes \(U_{nj} = \mathbf{X}_{nj}'\beta_n + \epsilon_{nj}\), where \(\beta_n \sim f(\beta | b, W)\) is a vector of coefficients for individual \(n\). The overall choice probability is the integral of the logit probabilities over the distribution of \(\beta_n\): $$ P_{ni} = \int \frac{e^{\mathbf{X}{ni}'\beta}}{\sum f(\beta | b, W) d\beta $$} e^{\mathbf{X}_{nj}'\beta}

docs.title: 4.1 Maximum Likelihood (for MNL and Nested Logit)
docs.text: For models with a closed-form choice probability, we can use standard Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

docs.title: 4.2 Maximum Simulated Likelihood (for Mixed Logit)
docs.text: For models without a closed-form probability like the Mixed Logit, we use Maximum Simulated Likelihood (MSL). We approximate the integral in the choice probability by taking many draws from the distribution of the random coefficients and averaging the resulting logit probabilities.

docs.title: 4.3 Bayesian Estimation via MCMC
docs.text: An alternative to MSL for Mixed Logit is to use Bayesian MCMC methods. This approach treats the individual-level coefficients \(\beta_n\) as latent variables to be estimated along with the population-level parameters \((b, W)\). It can be more computationally robust and provides a richer characterization of uncertainty.

docs.title: 5. Application: The BLP Model of Demand
docs.text:
The Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (BLP, 1995) model is the workhorse of modern empirical Industrial Organization. It combines a Mixed Logit demand model with instrumental variables to tackle the critical problem of price endogeneity (prices are correlated with unobserved product quality).

The BLP Algorithm: 1. Demand Side: A Mixed Logit model relates consumer choices to product characteristics (including price) and unobserved quality, \(\xi_j\). The model allows for heterogeneous consumer tastes. 2. Supply Side: Firms are assumed to set prices in a Bertrand-Nash equilibrium, where price is a function of marginal cost and the prices of competing products. 3. Inversion: The key insight is to use the model to invert the observed market shares to back out the unobserved product quality shocks, \(\xi_j\), that are consistent with the data. 4. GMM Estimation: The final step is a GMM estimation. The moment condition is that the unobserved quality shocks, \(\xi_j\), must be uncorrelated with the instrumental variables. Common instruments include the characteristics of other firms' products, which are correlated with price but plausibly uncorrelated with the unobserved quality of a specific product.

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
These relations are collected from the derivations above as a review map. Their assumptions and derivations remain part of the result; this box is not a substitute for them.

1. Core relation

\[U_{nj} = V_{nj} + \epsilon_{nj}\]

2. Core relation

\[P_{ni} = \text{Prob}(V_{ni} + \epsilon_{ni} > V_{nj} + \epsilon_{nj} \quad \forall j \neq i)\]

3. Core relation

\[P_{ni} = \frac{e^{V_{ni}}}{\sum_{j \in C_n} e^{V_{nj}}}\]

4. Core relation

\[P_{ni} = P(i | \text{nest } k) \times P(\text{nest } k)\]

docs.title: Three-Tier Practice Ladder
docs.text:
1. Mechanism and assumptions (Conceptual): Write the optimization or equilibrium problem underlying 04 Discrete Choice Models and derive its first-order, incentive, or market-clearing conditions. Discuss any relevant corner solution.

2. Reproduce and diagnose (Applied): Construct a small numerical example using 1. The Random Utility Model (RUM) Framework, 2. The Multinomial Logit (MNL). Verify feasibility and optimality/equilibrium conditions numerically rather than relying only on the solver status.

3. Robust extension (Challenge): Relax one substantive assumption—information, convexity, symmetry, commitment, or market completeness—and predict how equilibrium or welfare changes before computing the extension.

3b. Failure analysis (Challenge): Predicted mode shares stop summing to one after a new transit category is added, and the data clearly violate the red-bus/blue-bus independence pattern. Diagnose the IIA restriction of plain logit, repair with nested or mixed logit, and test the improvement with a Hausman-type comparison on the added alternative.

Use the existing exercises above when they target the same skill; this ladder makes the intended progression explicit rather than replacing instructor-authored problems.

docs.title: 6. Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• RUM: The Random Utility Model is the theoretical foundation, where choice probabilities are determined by the distribution of unobserved utility.
  • Logit Models: Assuming IID Gumbel errors yields the simple Multinomial Logit (MNL), but this implies the restrictive IIA property. The Nested Logit relaxes this by grouping alternatives, while the Mixed Logit is fully flexible by allowing for random taste coefficients.
  • Estimation: Simple logit models are estimated with MLE. More complex models like Mixed Logit require simulation methods, either Maximum Simulated Likelihood (MSL) or Bayesian MCMC.
  • Endogeneity: In real-world applications, price is often endogenous. The BLP model is the standard framework for tackling this, combining a Mixed Logit demand system with an instrumental variables (GMM) approach.

docs.title: 7. Exercises
docs.text:
1. The IIA Property: Explain the "red bus/blue bus" problem. Why does the Multinomial Logit model fail in this scenario, and how does the Nested Logit model solve the problem?

  2. Derivation of Logit: Show that if \(U_1 = V_1 + \epsilon_1\) and \(U_2 = V_2 + \epsilon_2\), where \(\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2\) are IID Gumbel, then the difference \(\epsilon_1 - \epsilon_2\) follows a logistic distribution, and from this, derive the binary logit choice probability.

  3. Simulation Bias: The MSL estimator is consistent, but it is biased in finite samples because of the simulation noise. How does the bias of the MSL estimator depend on the number of simulation draws, R?

  4. Welfare Calculation: The log-sum-exp term, \(\ln(\sum_j e^{V_{nj}})\), represents the expected maximum utility an individual gets from their choice set. Use estimated MNL parameters to calculate the change in consumer welfare (in dollar terms) if the price of one alternative increases by 10%. (Hint: The marginal utility of income is the negative of the price coefficient).

  5. BLP Instruments: In the BLP model, why are the characteristics of other firms' products considered a valid instrument for price? Explain both the relevance and exogeneity conditions in this context.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Discrete choice models link utility maximization to choice probabilities.

Key Takeaways: * Random Utility: Agents choose the option with the highest utility, but the econometrician only sees part of that utility. The rest is noise. * IIA Property: The Logit model assumes the ratio of probabilities between two alternatives is independent of other alternatives. This can be unrealistic (Red Bus/Blue Bus paradox). * BLP: The random coefficients logit (BLP) overcomes IIA and is the state-of-the-art for demand estimation.

docs.title: The Lens: The Economics of Incentives
docs.text:
What problem are we solving? When a Principal (boss) hires an Agent (worker), the boss cannot perfectly monitor the worker's effort. This information asymmetry creates Moral Hazard. How do you design a contract that aligns the worker's incentives with the firm's goals, without exposing them to too much risk?

Why this method? We solve a constrained optimization problem: maximize the Principal's profit subject to: 1. Participation Constraint (IR): The agent must accept the contract. 2. Incentive Compatibility (IC): The agent must voluntarily choose the effort level the Principal wants.

This notebook explores optimal contract design under asymmetric information.

Economic question. In 05 Principal Agent Models, what must remain economically invariant when the computational representation changes? The useful question is how preferences, technologies, information, or strategic beliefs map into choices and welfare, and whether the computed solution respects feasibility, optimality, and equilibrium conditions. Whenever multiple equilibria or corner solutions are possible, the numerical method should expose rather than hide that economic structure.

docs.title: 1.1 The Static Incentive-Insurance Trade-Off
docs.text:
In the canonical static model, a risk-neutral Principal hires a risk-averse Agent. The Principal's goal is to design a wage contract \((w_H, w_L)\) based on observable outcomes (high or low output) to induce unobservable high effort (\(e_H\)) at minimum cost.

The Principal faces a trade-off. To induce high effort, they must offer a wage spread (\(w_H > w_L\)), linking pay to performance. However, this exposes the risk-averse agent to income risk. The optimal second-best contract balances this incentive-insurance trade-off. It provides the minimum amount of incentive (and thus imposes the minimum amount of costly risk) needed to induce high effort.

docs.title: Interactive: The Incentive-Insurance Trade-Off
docs.text:
def solve_moral_hazard_numeric(pi_H=0.8, pi_L=0.3, c_H=1.0, u_bar=0.5, gamma=2.0):
    """Solves the moral hazard problem numerically."""
    u = lambda w: (w**(1 - gamma) - 1) / (1 - gamma) if not np.isclose(gamma, 1) else np.log(w)

    # Objective: Minimize principal's expected wage cost
    def objective(w):
        w_H, w_L = w
        return pi_H * w_H + (1 - pi_H) * w_L

    # Constraints
    constraints = [
        # 1. Incentive Compatibility (IC): Agent must prefer high effort
        {'type': 'ineq', 'fun': lambda w: (pi_H * u(w[0]) + (1 - pi_H) * u(w[1]) - c_H) - \
                                          (pi_L * u(w[0]) + (1 - pi_L) * u(w[1]))},
        # 2. Participation Constraint (PC): Agent must prefer working to outside option
        {'type': 'ineq', 'fun': lambda w: pi_H * u(w[0]) + (1 - pi_H) * u(w[1]) - c_H - u_bar}
    ]

    # Initial guess and bounds
    w0 = [10, 5]
    bounds = [(0.01, None), (0.01, None)]

    result = minimize(objective, w0, bounds=bounds, constraints=constraints)

    if result.success:
        w_H, w_L = result.x
        expected_wage = result.fun
        display(Markdown(f'> **Note:** For Agent RRA (γ) = {gamma:.1f}:'))
        print(f"  - Optimal Contract: w_H = ${w_H:.2f}, w_L = ${w_L:.2f}")
        print(f"  - Required Wage Spread (Incentive): ${w_H - w_L:.2f}")
        print(f"  - Expected Wage Cost to Principal: ${expected_wage:.2f}")
    else:
        display(Markdown(f'> **Note:** Optimization failed for gamma={gamma:.1f}. This may happen if the agent is too risk averse for a feasible contract to exist with these parameters.'))

widgets.interact(solve_moral_hazard_numeric,
                 pi_H=widgets.FloatSlider(min=0.5, max=0.95, step=0.05, value=0.8, description='Prob(High|Effort)'),
                 gamma=widgets.FloatSlider(min=0.5, max=5.0, step=0.5, value=2.0, description='Risk Aversion (γ)'));

docs.title: 1.2 The First-Order Approach (Continuous Effort)
docs.text:
When effort is a continuous choice, the Principal's problem can often be simplified by replacing the agent's full incentive compatibility constraint with just its first-order condition. This first-order approach is valid if the agent's optimization problem is concave, which is ensured by the Convexity of the Distribution Function Condition (CDFC).

This approach leads to the elegant Mirrlees-Holmström condition, which states that the agent's inverse marginal utility of income should be a linear function of the likelihood ratio: $$ \frac{1}{u'(w(q))} = \lambda + \mu \frac{f_e(q|e)}{f(q|e)} $$ The term \(\frac{f_e(q|e)}{f(q|e)}\) is the score of the likelihood function. It measures how informative output \(q\) is about the agent's effort. The optimal contract makes pay most sensitive to outcomes that are most informative about effort.

docs.title: 1.3 Dynamic Moral Hazard
docs.text: In a multi-period relationship, the Principal has another tool: the promise of future rewards. The Principal can use the agent's continuation value as an incentive device. A good outcome today can be rewarded not just with a higher wage, but with a promotion or the continuation of a profitable relationship. This allows the Principal to rely less on direct, risky wage incentives in any single period, leading to better risk-sharing. This is the logic behind efficiency wages and career concerns.

docs.title: 2.1 The Optimal Screening Menu
docs.text:
Here, the Agent has hidden information about their "type" before signing a contract. The Principal's challenge is to design a menu of contracts that induces agents to sort themselves correctly. The canonical example is a monopolist selling a product to consumers with different valuations.

The solution involves a trade-off between efficiency and information rent extraction. The typical result is: 1. Efficiency at the Top: The high-value type is offered the socially efficient quantity. 2. Downward Distortion: The low-value type is offered an inefficiently low quantity to make their contract less attractive to the high type. 3. No Rent at the Bottom: The low-value type gets zero surplus. 4. Information Rent for the High Type: The high-value type gets a positive surplus, as the Principal must leave them with enough surplus to prevent them from pretending to be a low type.

docs.title: Visualizing the Adverse Selection Solution
docs.text:
# --- Model Parameters ---
# theta_H: High type's valuation parameter
# theta_L: Low type's valuation parameter
# c: Marginal cost of production

def u(q, theta): return theta * np.sqrt(q)
def solve_screening_problem(theta_H=10, theta_L=5, c=1):
    q_fb_H = (theta_H / (2 * c))**2
    q_sb_L = ((2*theta_L - theta_H) / (2 * c))**2 if (2*theta_L > theta_H) else 0
    p_sb_L = u(q_sb_L, theta_L)
    p_sb_H = u(q_fb_H, theta_H) - (u(q_sb_L, theta_H) - p_sb_L)
    return (q_fb_H, p_sb_H), (q_sb_L, p_sb_L)

(qH, pH), (qL, pL) = solve_screening_problem()

display(Markdown(f"> **Note:** Optimal Menu: High type gets ({qH:.2f} units for ${pH:.2f}). Low type gets ({qL:.2f} units for ${pL:.2f})."))

q_grid = np.linspace(0.01, 100, 200)
plt.figure(figsize=(12,8))
plt.plot(q_grid, u(q_grid, 10), 'b-', label='High Type IC')
plt.plot(q_grid, u(q_grid, 5), 'g-', label='Low Type IC')
plt.plot(q_grid, u(q_grid, 10) - u(qL, 10) + pL, 'b--', label='High Type IC through (qL, pL)')
plt.plot([qH, qL], [pH, pL], 'ro', markersize=12, label='Offered Contracts')
plt.title('Screening: Optimal Menu of Contracts'); plt.xlabel('Quantity (q)'); plt.ylabel('Payment (p)')
plt.legend(); plt.grid(True); plt.ylim(0, 80); plt.show()

docs.title: 2.2 The Revelation Principle
docs.text: A foundational result in mechanism design is the Revelation Principle. It states that any outcome that can be achieved by any mechanism (no matter how complex) can also be achieved by a direct, incentive-compatible mechanism where agents truthfully report their private information. This dramatically simplifies the search for an optimal mechanism, as we only need to consider the much smaller class of direct, truthful mechanisms.

docs.title: 3. Application: Optimal Unemployment Insurance
docs.text:
The design of an optimal unemployment insurance (UI) system is a classic principal-agent problem. The government (Principal) wants to provide insurance to risk-averse workers (Agents) against job loss. However, this creates moral hazard: generous UI benefits may reduce an agent's incentive to search for a new job.

The Baily-Chetty formula characterizes the optimal UI replacement rate, \(b\), balancing this trade-off: $$ \frac{u'(c_e) - u'(c_u)}{u'(c_e)} = \frac{\epsilon_s}{\eta_b} $$ Where \(c_e\) and \(c_u\) are consumption when employed and unemployed, \(\epsilon_s\) is the elasticity of unemployment duration with respect to benefits, and \(\eta_b\) is the mechanical effect of benefits on the government budget. The formula says that the marginal benefit of insurance (LHS) should equal the marginal cost of distorted incentives (RHS).

docs.title: 4. Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• Asymmetric Information is a core source of market friction, leading to problems of Moral Hazard (hidden action) and Adverse Selection (hidden information).
  • Moral Hazard contracts must balance providing incentives against imposing costly risk on risk-averse agents. In dynamic settings, continuation values can also be used as an incentive device.
  • Adverse Selection problems are solved by designing a menu of contracts that induces agents to self-select based on their private information. This typically involves distorting the allocation for low types to reduce the information rent paid to high types.
  • The Revelation Principle is a powerful theoretical tool that simplifies the design of optimal mechanisms.
  • Applications of principal-agent theory are vast, covering everything from executive compensation and insurance design to optimal taxation and regulation.

  • Incentive compatibility: the recommended action must maximize the agent's expected utility among feasible actions.
  • Principal objective: maximize expected output net of compensation subject to participation and incentive constraints.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Incentives matter. Principal-Agent theory quantifies the cost of motivating people.

Key Takeaways: * Risk-Incentive Trade-off: Stronger incentives (paying for performance) induce higher effort but expose the risk-averse agent to more income volatility. * Second Best: We cannot achieve the "First Best" (perfect information) outcome. The cost of agency is the risk premium paid to the agent or the efficiency loss from lower effort. * Applications: Executive compensation, insurance deductibles, and sharecropping are all real-world solutions to agency problems.

docs.title: The Lens: When Markets Fail
docs.text:
What problem are we solving? The First Welfare Theorem assumes everyone knows everything about the goods they trade. But what if the seller knows more than the buyer? Information Economics studies how asymmetric information destroys markets. * Adverse Selection: "Lemons" drive good cars out of the market (Akerlof). * Signaling: High-quality agents burn money (degrees, ads) to prove their worth (Spence). * Screening: Principals design menus of contracts to separate agent types (Stiglitz).

This notebook models the unraveling of markets and the mechanisms that restore them.

Economic question. In 06 Information Economics, what must remain economically invariant when the computational representation changes? Microeconomic computation makes equilibrium and incentive constraints operational. The useful question is how preferences, technologies, information, or strategic beliefs map into choices and welfare, and whether the computed solution respects feasibility, optimality, and equilibrium conditions. Whenever multiple equilibria or corner solutions are possible, the numerical method should expose rather than hide that economic structure.
